entries.title: LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation
entries.body:
LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation

## Symptom

Passing `ResponseFormat.JSON` (type only, no schema) to `ChatRequest.builder().responseFormat(...)` for an Anthropic-backed `ChatModel` throws `UnsupportedFeatureException` rather than silently degrading or prompting.

## Context

`InternalAnthropicHelper.validate(ChatRequestParameters)` is called inside `AnthropicChatModel.doChat()` before any API call is made. The validation checks:

```java
if (parameters.responseFormat() != null
        && parameters.responseFormat().type() == ResponseFormatType.JSON
        && parameters.responseFormat().jsonSchema() == null) {
    throw new UnsupportedFeatureException(...);
}
```

This means JSON mode without a schema is explicitly rejected at the LangChain4j layer — it never reaches the Anthropic API.

## Root cause

Anthropic's native API requires a JSON schema to enforce structured output. Unlike OpenAI (which supports a bare JSON mode that produces valid but unstructured JSON), Anthropic has no schema-less JSON mode. LangChain4j's Anthropic integration reflects this correctly by refusing the schemaless request rather than silently ignoring the constraint.

## Fix

Always pair `ResponseFormat.JSON` with a `JsonSchema` when using Anthropic:

```java
ResponseFormat responseFormat = ResponseFormat.builder()
    .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
    .jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
        .name("MySchema")
        .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
            .addStringProperty("field", "Description")
            .required("field")
            .build())
        .build())
    .build();
```

For a broad catch on provider-specific failures (including older Claude models that don't support structured output at all), wrap the `llm.chat(request)` call in `catch (Exception e)` and degrade gracefully:

```java
try {
    ChatResponse response = llm.chat(request);
    return Optional.of(parse(response.aiMessage().text()));
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("Structured enrichment failed ({}), falling back to structural rendering", e.getMessage());
    return Optional.empty();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The LangChain4j docs describe `ResponseFormat.JSON` as a valid type value. There is no public documentation on which providers support it with or without a schema. The `UnsupportedFeatureException` is thrown before any network call, so there is no HTTP error to debug — it looks like an in-process configuration error with no obvious connection to the Anthropic API's structured output requirements.

The `supportedCapabilities()` mechanism exists on `ChatModel` for high-level AI Services to check before using JSON schema, but `ClaudeMarkdownRenderer`-style code calling the low-level `ChatModel.chat(ChatRequest)` API bypasses that guard entirely.

### Why this fix

`ResponseFormat.JSON` with `JsonSchema` is the only valid combination for Anthropic. Adding a schema is not optional — it is the required API surface.

langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types
entries.body:
langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types

### What it is
`DeclarativeUtil` in `langchain4j-agentic` exposes a single static list `chatSupplierParameterResolvers` with one registration method `addChatSupplierParameterResolver(ChatSupplierParameterResolver)`. This resolver hook fires only during `@ChatModelSupplier` and `@StreamingChatModelSupplier` processing. All other supplier annotations (`@ToolsSupplier`, `@ChatMemorySupplier`, `@ChatMemoryProviderSupplier`, `@ContentRetrieverSupplier`, `@RetrievalAugmentorSupplier`, `@AgentListenerSupplier`, `@ToolProviderSupplier`) call `checkArguments(method)` which enforces **zero parameters** before invoking the static method directly — no resolver hook exists for these paths.

### Why this matters for framework integrators
Any DI framework (Quarkus, Spring, Guice) wanting to inject CDI/Spring beans into supplier methods is blocked for all supplier types except chat model suppliers. The `@CdiBean` workaround in `quarkus-langchain4j` only works for `@ChatModelSupplier` as a result. Users who need a CDI-managed `ContentRetriever` or `ChatMemory` must use `Arc.container()` or `ApplicationContext.getBean()` inside the static method body — bypassing injection, scope management, and testability.

### How to discover this
Only by decompiling `langchain4j-agentic-1.15.1-beta25.jar` and reading `DeclarativeUtil.class`. The library has no published Javadoc for internal classes and no documentation of the SPI surface area.

```bash
# Locate the JAR
find ~/.m2/repository/dev/langchain4j/langchain4j-agentic -name "*.jar" | grep -v sources | head -1

# The class structure reveals: addChatSupplierParameterResolver() is the only hook
# All other configureAgent() branches call checkArguments() then invokeStatic()
```

### Workaround
For Quarkus: use `SyntheticCreationalContext.getInjectedReference()` in the synthetic bean creator (`AgenticRecorder`) to inject CDI beans at agent construction time, bypassing the static supplier method entirely. This requires detecting at build time that no static supplier method exists for a given type, then adding a CDI injection point for that type.

### Upstream path
An upstream PR to `langchain4j-agentic` should propose a general `SupplierParameterResolver` SPI (not chat-model-specific) and add resolver hooks to all supplier type branches in `configureAgent()`. Frame as a DI-framework-agnostic improvement — Spring users would benefit from the same hook.

### Why this is non-obvious
The library name suggests platform independence (`langchain4j` not `langchain4j-spring`), so the assumption is that all supplier types are equally extensible. The asymmetry between `@ChatModelSupplier` (has a resolver hook) and all other supplier annotations (do not) is not mentioned in any README, Javadoc, or issue tracker. The class is package-private in the library with no stable API guarantee.

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j-anthropic 0.26.1 fails with 'Run time configuration cannot be consumed in Build Steps' on Quarkus 3.33+
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j-anthropic 0.26.1 fails with 'Run time configuration cannot be consumed in Build Steps' on Quarkus 3.33+

## Symptom

Quarkus augmentation fails immediately with:

```
Failed to load steps from class io.quarkiverse.langchain4j.anthropic.deployment.AnthropicProcessor:
Run time configuration cannot be consumed in Build Steps,
use RuntimeValue<io.quarkiverse.langchain4j.anthropic.runtime.config.LangChain4jAnthropicConfig>
in a @Recorder constructor instead
```

No application code runs. The error appears before any Quarkus startup.

## Context

Adding `quarkus-langchain4j-anthropic 0.26.1` as a dependency to a Quarkus 3.33+ project. No changes to application code — the failure occurs at the Quarkus deployment phase.

## Root Cause

`AnthropicProcessor` in 0.26.1 directly injects `LangChain4jAnthropicConfig` into a `@BuildStep` method parameter. In Quarkus 3.33+, the augmentation API prohibits direct config injection in build steps — it must use `RuntimeValue<T>` via a `@Recorder`. This API change was introduced to enforce the build-time / runtime separation more strictly.

The error message describes a *user code* problem ("use RuntimeValue in a @Recorder constructor") but the actual problem is inside the library.

## Fix

Use `quarkus-langchain4j-anthropic 1.9.1` instead of 0.26.1. Version 1.9.1 was compiled against Quarkus 3.33.1 and uses `RuntimeValue<>` correctly:

```xml
<!-- parent pom.xml -->
<!-- 0.26.1 incompatible with Quarkus 3.33+; 1.9.1 built against 3.33.1, verified on 3.34.3 -->
<quarkus-langchain4j.version>1.9.1</quarkus-langchain4j.version>
```

```xml
<!-- module pom.xml -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.quarkiverse.langchain4j</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-langchain4j-anthropic</artifactId>
  <version>${quarkus-langchain4j.version}</version>
</dependency>
```

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

"Run time configuration cannot be consumed in Build Steps" sounds like a developer mistake — putting `@Inject` in the wrong place, or misconfiguring a custom extension. Nothing in the error message mentions a version number or suggests the cause is inside a dependency. The version `0.26.1` carries no numeric hint that it is incompatible with Quarkus 3.33+. A developer reading the error would audit their own code first, then check their own extensions, before suspecting the LangChain4j library itself.

entries.title: langchain4j-embeddings uses independent versioning from main langchain4j — version 1.14.1 does not exist
entries.body:
langchain4j-embeddings uses independent versioning from main langchain4j — version 1.14.1 does not exist

### Symptom
Maven build fails when `langchain4j-embeddings` is declared with `${langchain4j.version}` (e.g. 1.14.1):

```
Could not collect dependencies: Failed to read artifact descriptor for
dev.langchain4j:langchain4j-embeddings:jar:1.14.1
```

The artifact is reported as "absent" from Maven Central, then falls through to other repositories (e.g. GitHub Packages) which return 401 Unauthorized — misleading the developer into thinking it's an auth problem.

### Context
`dev.langchain4j:langchain4j-embeddings` provides `OnnxEmbeddingModel` for running in-process ONNX embedding models. It was originally in a separate repository (`langchain4j/langchain4j-embeddings`) with its own release cycle. It has since been moved into the main `langchain4j` repository under `embeddings/`, but Maven Central artifacts still follow the independent version scheme.

Available versions on Maven Central: 0.17.0 through 0.36.2, then 1.0.0-alpha1 through 1.0.0-beta5. No version matching the main langchain4j line (1.14.x, 1.15.x, etc.) exists.

### What was tried (didn't work)
1. Using `${langchain4j.version}` (1.14.1) — artifact does not exist
2. Guessing `1.14.1-beta22` — does not exist either
3. Searching Maven Central search API — confirmed only 31 versions exist, none in the 1.14.x range

### Root cause
The `langchain4j-embeddings` module uses a completely independent versioning scheme from the main `langchain4j` library. The parent POM in the LangChain4j repository shows a `-betaN` suffix on the parent version (e.g. `1.17.0-beta27-SNAPSHOT`), but published artifacts stop at `1.0.0-beta5`.

### Fix
Declare a separate version property for `langchain4j-embeddings`:

```xml
<properties>
    <langchain4j.version>1.14.1</langchain4j.version>
    <langchain4j-embeddings.version>1.0.0-beta5</langchain4j-embeddings.version>
</properties>

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>dev.langchain4j</groupId>
            <artifactId>langchain4j-embeddings</artifactId>
            <version>${langchain4j-embeddings.version}</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
```

The `1.0.0-beta5` jar depends on `langchain4j-core:1.0.0` but is binary compatible with `langchain4j-core:1.14.1` — the `EmbeddingModel` interface is stable within 1.x. Transitive deps (`onnxruntime`, `ai.djl.huggingface:tokenizers`) are overridden by your project's dependency management.

### Why this is non-obvious
The LangChain4j ecosystem uses a single version number for all core modules (`langchain4j`, `langchain4j-core`, `langchain4j-qdrant`, etc.) and the BOM covers them. The embeddings modules are the exception — they have their own version line. Nothing in the documentation or the parent POM structure signals this. The natural assumption is `${langchain4j.version}` works for everything.

### Why this fix
Using a separate version property rather than pinning in the child POM keeps the version centrally managed and signals that this artifact is intentionally on a different version line.

### Alternatives considered
- Using a pre-packaged model artifact (e.g. `langchain4j-embeddings-all-minilm-l6-v2`) — bundles the model in the jar, but we need to download models separately for different deployment targets.
- Building an `EmbeddingModel` adapter on top of the inference-runtime module — overengineering; LangChain4j already provides this capability via `OnnxEmbeddingModel`.

**See also:** [GE-20260621-cb4492](GE-20260621-cb4492.md) — drools-engine artifact does not exist at Drools 10.1.0 — use drools-model-codegen (same artifact-rename pattern)

entries.title: langchain4j-document-parser-apache-tika artifact doesn't exist for LangChain4j 1.14.1
entries.body:
langchain4j-document-parser-apache-tika artifact doesn't exist for LangChain4j 1.14.1

# langchain4j-document-parser-apache-tika artifact doesn't exist for LangChain4j 1.14.1

## Symptom

Maven dependency resolution fails for `dev.langchain4j:langchain4j-document-parser-apache-tika:1.14.1` with "Could not find artifact" error.

## Context

Adding Tika document parsing to a LangChain4j RAG pipeline. Examples and tutorials reference the `langchain4j-document-parser-apache-tika` module as the standard way to parse PDFs, Word docs, etc. into LangChain4j `Document` objects.

## What was tried

- Verified LangChain4j core version (1.14.1) is available in Maven Central — it is
- Searched Maven Central for the artifact — `langchain4j-document-parser-apache-tika` exists for some versions but not 1.14.1
- Checked LangChain4j release notes — no mention of the document parser modules being removed

## Root cause

The document parser modules were restructured in LangChain4j — they use a different versioning scheme and may not be published for all LangChain4j core versions. The artifact name in older examples may refer to a module that existed in earlier releases but was deprecated, renamed, or not built for newer versions.

As of LangChain4j 1.14.1, the Tika parser module either:
- Was not published to Maven Central for this version
- Uses a different artifact ID
- Has been replaced by direct Tika integration

## Fix

Use Apache Tika directly and integrate manually with LangChain4j's `Document` and `DocumentSplitter` APIs:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.tika</groupId>
    <artifactId>tika-core</artifactId>
    <version>2.9.2</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.tika</groupId>
    <artifactId>tika-parsers-standard-package</artifactId>
    <version>2.9.2</version>
</dependency>
```

Parse documents and wrap results:

```java
Tika tika = new Tika();
String content = tika.parseToString(inputStream);
Document doc = Document.from(content, metadata);
```

## Why non-obvious

LangChain4j documentation and tutorials reference `langchain4j-document-parser-apache-tika` as if it's always available alongside the core library. The version mismatch is only discovered at Maven resolution time — there's no compile-time or runtime indication that the module doesn't exist until the build fails.

The LangChain4j GitHub repo may have the source for these modules, but they're not being published to Maven Central for all core releases.

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama added via Maven test-scope profile requires mvn clean to invalidate augmentation cache

## Symptom

After adding `quarkus-langchain4j-ollama` as a test-scope dependency inside a Maven profile
(`-Peval-ollama`), the Ollama `ChatModel` bean is not registered. Config keys are logged as
`Unrecognized configuration key "quarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name"`, and the
test fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for `ChatModel`.

## Context

The module was previously built without the Ollama extension. Maven resolves the Ollama JAR
when the profile is active, but Quarkus reuses its disk-based augmentation cache from the
prior build — before the Ollama extension was on the classpath. The Ollama extension is
silently absent from augmentation: no beans registered, no config processors active.

## What was tried (didn't work)

- Running `mvn test -Peval,eval-ollama` after the JAR appeared in `~/.m2` — stale augmentation
  cache persisted, config keys still unrecognized.
- Adding `-Dquarkus.test.profile=eval` explicitly — no effect on cache.

## Root cause

Quarkus augmentation is disk-cached in `target/quarkus-app/`. When classpath changes occur
(new extension added via Maven profile), the cache invalidation heuristic does not always
detect the change, especially when the Ollama JAR was already present in `~/.m2` from a
prior `mvn dependency:resolve` call (updating file timestamps). The cache is reused, and
the Ollama extension's CDI beans are never registered.

## Fix

Run `mvn clean` before the first test run with the new profile:

```bash
JAVA_HOME=$(/usr/libexec/java_home -v 26) mvn clean test -pl eval -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dtest=PromptEvalTest#evaluateRealWorldScenarios \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.model-name=qwen3:8b" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.chat-model.format=json" \
  "-Dquarkus.langchain4j.ollama.timeout=300s"
```

Subsequent runs without `clean` work correctly — the Ollama-aware augmentation is now cached.

## Why this is non-obvious

The "unrecognized configuration key" warning does not hint at augmentation caching — it reads
as though the extension was not added at all, not that a stale build artifact is in play.
The Ollama JAR is visible in `mvn dependency:resolve` output, making the missing registration
doubly confusing. The standard fix for missing CDI beans (`check your imports, check your
annotations`) leads nowhere.

**See also:** [GE-20260530-0178fd](GE-20260530-0178fd.md) — Quarkus @QuarkusTest augmentation requires extension deployment JARs in ~/.m2 | [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension @Default ChatModel clashes with @DefaultBean

entries.title: @Alternative @Priority(1) beans in a test-helper jar are invisible to downstream @QuarkusTest — no Jandex index
entries.body:
@Alternative @Priority(1) beans in a test-helper jar are invisible to downstream @QuarkusTest — no Jandex index

## Context

Building a `casehub-testing` module to provide `@Alternative @Priority(1)` in-memory repository implementations that downstream `@QuarkusTest` classes can consume by just adding the module as a test dependency — no `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` config needed.

## Symptom

```
jakarta.enterprise.inject.UnsatisfiedResolutionException: Unsatisfied dependency
  for type io.casehub.engine.spi.CaseInstanceRepository and qualifiers [@Default]
```

Downstream `@QuarkusTest` fails to start even though `casehub-testing` is on the classpath and its `TestCaseInstanceRepository` carries `@Alternative @Priority(1) @ApplicationScoped`.

## Root Cause

Quarkus CDI bean discovery requires a Jandex index to scan beans from classpath JARs. If the testing helper JAR does not build a Jandex index (i.e., the `jandex-maven-plugin` or equivalent is not configured), Quarkus cannot see any of its beans — including `@Alternative @Priority(1)` classes. The annotation is present in the bytecode but the JAR is effectively invisible to CDI.

The `casehub-testing` pom.xml had no Jandex configuration, so its beans were never indexed.

## Fix

**Option A (recommended for reusable testing jars):** Add Jandex indexing to the helper module's pom.xml:

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>io.smallrye</groupId>
    <artifactId>jandex-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <id>make-index</id>
            <goals><goal>jandex</goal></goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

**Option B (proven fallback):** Keep in-memory implementations in `casehub-persistence-memory` without `@Priority`, and activate them via `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `src/test/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseInstanceRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryEventLogRepository
```

Option B is what every other module in the project already uses and is the safe, proven path.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The `@Alternative @Priority(1)` pattern is supposed to be self-activating — you expect it to "just work" when the JAR is on the classpath. The failure message says "unsatisfied dependency" which points to a missing implementation, not to a missing index. Nothing in the error or Quarkus startup log mentions Jandex.

**See also:** [GE-20260423-a01832](GE-20260423-a01832.md) — @Alternative beans in third-party test jars not scanned without explicit index config | [GE-20260421-03fa72](GE-20260421-03fa72.md) — optional module jar missing Jandex index | [GE-20260417-c59817](GE-20260417-c59817.md) — quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives activates @Alternative beans | [GE-20260427-62d3ab](GE-20260427-62d3ab.md) — @Alternative @Priority(1) inner beans as test spies | [GE-20260424-59906a](GE-20260424-59906a.md) — CDI does not scan @ApplicationScoped beans in plain JAR module | [GE-0133](GE-0133.md) — CDI silently ignores beans in jars without Jandex index

**See also:** GE-20260422-ebb91d — CDI AmbiguousResolutionException when multiple @ApplicationScoped beans implement the same SPI interface
**See also:** [GE-20260415-884e48 — @Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException](GE-20260415-884e48.md)

entries.body:
@Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException

## @Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException

### Stack
Quarkus 3.31.1, CDI 4.0

### Symptom
Multiple beans implement the same SPI interface. Each alternative is annotated with
`@Alternative @Priority(10)` as well as `@ApplicationScoped`. On Quarkus startup, the
application fails with `AmbiguousResolutionException` — all implementations are active
simultaneously.

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ContextDiffStrategy
and qualifiers [@Default]: [TopLevelContextDiffStrategy, JsonPatchContextDiffStrategy, 
NoOpContextDiffStrategy]
```

### Context
SPI pattern where one default bean and two `@Alternative` beans implement an interface.
The intent was to activate one alternative at a time via
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `application.properties`.

### What was tried
Adding `@Priority(10)` alongside `@Alternative` — expected this to be a ranking hint
that would help CDI resolve ambiguity. Instead, `@Priority` on an `@Alternative` is what
globally activates the bean in CDI 4.0, making all three implementations simultaneously
active and causing the ambiguous resolution error.

### Root cause
In CDI 4.0 (Jakarta EE 10), `@Alternative @Priority(n)` is a shorthand for globally
activating an alternative across the entire application — no `beans.xml` or
`selected-alternatives` config needed. When ALL alternatives carry this annotation,
they are ALL active, which breaks injection points expecting a single bean.

### Solution 1 — Remove @Priority, use selected-alternatives config
**Approach:** Strip `@Priority` from all alternatives; activate one via config.
**Pros:** Per-profile/per-module control without code changes; the intended Quarkus mechanism for SPI switching.
**Cons:** Requires a config entry per activation; all alternatives default to inactive.

Remove `@Priority` from all `@Alternative` beans. Activate a specific alternative only
via `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `application.properties`:

```java
// WRONG — @Priority globally activates the alternative in CDI 4.0
@Alternative
@Priority(10)
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyAlternativeImpl implements MyInterface { ... }

// CORRECT — @Alternative only; activation controlled by config
@Alternative
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyAlternativeImpl implements MyInterface { ... }
```

```properties
# application.properties — activate the desired alternative
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.MyAlternativeImpl
```

### Solution 2 — Use different @Priority values to establish precedence
**Approach:** Keep `@Alternative @Priority` but assign distinct priority values; CDI resolves to the highest.
**Pros:** No config entry needed; the default (lowest priority) is always active, the override (highest priority) wins when present on the classpath. Works naturally for optional-module patterns where a higher-capability implementation should auto-replace the baseline.
**Cons:** All alternatives are always globally active (the core CDI 4.0 behaviour). The "default" must have the lowest priority; adding a third implementation requires careful priority assignment.

```java
// Default — always active; lowest priority loses when a higher one is present
@Alternative
@Priority(0)
@ApplicationScoped
public class ClaimFirstStrategy implements WorkerSelectionStrategy { ... }

// Override — higher priority wins; active only when on the classpath
@Alternative
@Priority(1)
@ApplicationScoped
public class SemanticWorkerSelectionStrategy implements WorkerSelectionStrategy { ... }
```

CDI injects the `@Priority(1)` bean when both are present; falls back to `@Priority(0)` when only
the default module is on the classpath. No `beans.xml` or `selected-alternatives` required.

**When to choose Solution 2 over Solution 1:** When the override is an optional module (not always
on the classpath) and the default must always be present. Config-based activation (Solution 1)
requires an explicit entry even for the default case; priority-based resolution (Solution 2) makes
the default zero-configuration.

### Why this is non-obvious
The `@Priority` annotation is commonly used alongside `@Alternative` in CDI tutorials
and examples from the CDI 2.x era, where `@Priority` on an alternative was a *ranking*
hint. In CDI 4.0 the semantics changed — `@Priority` on an `@Alternative` is now an
*activation* mechanism (equivalent to listing it in `beans.xml` with a priority). The
Quarkus docs for `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` don't warn about this interaction.

### Why this fix
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` gives per-profile/per-module control via config,
which is the intended Quarkus mechanism for SPI switching (same as how `PanningStrategyLoopControl`
and other engine SPIs are activated). It doesn't require code changes to switch backends.

**See also:** GE-20260422-ebb91d — AmbiguousResolutionException from multiple unqualified @ApplicationScoped beans

**See also:** GE-20260427-97650e "CDI ambiguity when adding second implementation of a quarkus-ledger repository interface"
**See also:** GE-20260427-62d3ab — use @Alternative @Priority(1) inner beans in @QuarkusTest to spy on SPI call sites
**See also:** [GE-20260427-c2b84f — @Alternative @Priority(1) beans in a test-helper jar are invisible to downstream @QuarkusTest — no Jandex index](GE-20260427-c2b84f.md)

### Update — Test-refactoring trap: two classes declaring the same @Alternative

During a test refactoring, if two `@QuarkusTest` classes *simultaneously* declare an
`@Alternative @Priority(2)` inner class implementing the same type, Quarkus boot fails
with `AmbiguousResolutionException` even though `mvn test-compile` passes cleanly. The
compile succeeds because both classes are syntactically valid; the CDI conflict only
surfaces at application startup.

entries.body:
@Alternative @Priority(1) from an external JAR does not override a non-alternative bean in Quarkus — needs exclude-types + selected-alternatives

## Symptom

Test assertions calling `workItemStore.scanAll()` return empty even though the handler log confirms `WorkItemService.create()` ran successfully. `planItem.getStatus()` is `RUNNING` (proving the handler completed), but the store shows nothing.

## Context

Two `WorkItemStore` beans on the test classpath:
- `JpaWorkItemStore @ApplicationScoped` — production bean from `casehub-work`
- `InMemoryWorkItemStore @Alternative @Priority(1)` — test replacement from `casehub-work-testing`

CDI 4.x spec says `@Priority` on an alternative activates it globally and it should win over non-alternatives. In Quarkus ARC 3.32.2 this does not hold when the alternative comes from an external dependency JAR.

## What was tried

- Adding `InMemoryWorkItemStore` to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` alone → "Ambiguous dependencies" deployment failure (both beans active simultaneously)
- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.work.runtime.repository.jpa.JpaWorkItemStore` alone → no effect; `JpaWorkItemStore` still wins
- `@Inject InMemoryWorkItemStore workItemStore` (concrete type) in the test → bypasses CDI alternative selection; test clears the right store but `WorkItemService` still writes to JPA (H2), so `scanAll()` returns empty

## Root Cause

`@Alternative @Priority(1)` from a dependency JAR is not treated as overriding a non-alternative `@ApplicationScoped` bean by Quarkus ARC. CDI spec §2.6.2 requires `@Priority` alternatives to take precedence, but ARC's resolution appears to treat both as equally active candidates when neither is the local application class. The non-alternative wins or ambiguity is raised.

## Fix

Combine both in `src/test/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
# Remove the JPA impl from CDI discovery entirely
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.work.runtime.repository.jpa.JpaWorkItemStore

# Explicitly select the in-memory replacement
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.work.testing.InMemoryWorkItemStore,\
  ...other alternatives...
```

With `JpaWorkItemStore` excluded, `InMemoryWorkItemStore` is the only active `WorkItemStore` bean. Explicit `selected-alternatives` listing then activates it. Both `WorkItemService` (via `@Inject WorkItemStore`) and the test (via `@Inject InMemoryWorkItemStore`) now reference the same singleton, and `scanAll()` finds what `create()` stored.

## Why this is non-obvious

CDI 4.x spec (and Quarkus docs on alternatives) state that `@Alternative @Priority(n)` globally activates and prioritises the alternative. A developer familiar with CDI 4.x would expect `@Priority(1)` to simply work. The failure is silent — no warning is emitted, `JpaWorkItemStore` just wins quietly. The symptom (empty `scanAll()`) points toward a different root cause (session caching, test isolation) and sends debugging in the wrong direction.

**See also:** [GE-20260429-a79d0e](GE-20260429-a79d0e.md) — @Alternative @Priority auto-activates within same module | [GE-20260521-4de4f1](GE-20260521-4de4f1.md) — TestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives() replaces selected-alternatives entirely

**See also:** [GE-20260601-cee623](GE-20260601-cee623.md) — QuarkusTestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives() replaces selected-alternatives entirely

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260616-d70e7e](GE-20260616-d70e7e.md) — selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans

entries.title: Quarkus ARC @DefaultBean injection points resolve before @Alternative activation in external JARs
entries.body:
Quarkus ARC @DefaultBean injection points resolve before @Alternative activation in external JARs

### Symptom

A `@DefaultBean` reactive bridge (`BlockingToReactiveCbrBridge`) that injects a blocking SPI interface (`CbrCaseMemoryStore`) silently resolves to the no-op `@DefaultBean` implementation (`NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore`) instead of the `@Alternative @Priority(2)` in-memory implementation (`InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore`), even when:

- The alternative is listed in `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`
- Both JARs are indexed via `quarkus.index-dependency`
- Direct injection of the blocking interface in a test class correctly resolves to the alternative

The retrieval returns empty with no error or warning — completely silent.

### Context

This occurs when three beans implement the same interface across two external JARs:

- **JAR A** (`casehub-neocortex-memory`): `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore` (`@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped`) and `BlockingToReactiveCbrBridge` (`@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped`, injects `CbrCaseMemoryStore`)
- **JAR B** (`casehub-neocortex-memory-cbr-inmem`): `InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore` (`@Alternative @Priority(2) @ApplicationScoped`)

The bridge in JAR A is supposed to delegate to whichever `CbrCaseMemoryStore` is active. When `InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore` is activated via `selected-alternatives`, direct injection works — but the bridge's own injection point does not.

### What was tried (didn't work)

1. Adding `quarkus.index-dependency` for both JARs — no effect on resolution
2. Adding `InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore` to `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in the memory profile — direct injection works, bridge delegation does not
3. Adding `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` for `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore` — breaks CDI wiring entirely (the bridge has no delegate)

### Root cause

Quarkus ARC resolves `@DefaultBean` beans' injection points at build time. When the bridge (`@DefaultBean`) is being wired, ARC resolves its `@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore` using the standard `@DefaultBean` resolution rules — which picks the other `@DefaultBean` (`NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore`) in the same JAR. The `@Alternative` from the external JAR is not considered for the bridge's injection point even though it would be selected for direct injection sites.

Confirmed via `System.identityHashCode()` tracing: both the test's `@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore` and the bridge's `@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore delegate` resolve to the same `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore_ClientProxy` instance.

### Solution 1 — Bypass the reactive bridge

**Approach:** Inject the blocking interface directly and offload to a worker thread.

**Pros:** No CDI resolution ambiguity. Works with any test profile.

**Cons:** Caller must handle thread offloading explicitly.

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyService {
    @Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore cbrStore; // blocking, not reactive

public Uni<List<Result>> retrieve(Query query) {
        return Uni.createFrom()
            .item(() -> cbrStore.retrieveSimilar(query, MyCase.class))
            .runSubscriptionOn(Infrastructure.getDefaultWorkerPool())
            .map(this::mapResults);
    }
}
```

### Solution 2 — Use QuarkusTestProfile.getEnabledAlternatives()

**Approach:** Override alternatives programmatically in the test profile.

**Pros:** Properly activates @Alternative beans for all injection points including bridge delegates.

**Cons:** `getEnabledAlternatives()` REPLACES (not appends to) `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` — ALL alternatives from the base profile must be re-declared. Missing one breaks other tests sharing the profile.

```java
public static class MemoryProfile implements QuarkusTestProfile {
    @Override
    public String getConfigProfile() { return "memory"; }

@Override
    public Set<Class<?>> getEnabledAlternatives() {
        return Set.of(
            InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository.class,
            InMemoryReactiveCaseMetaModelRepository.class,
            // ... ALL other memory profile alternatives ...
            InMemoryCbrCaseMemoryStore.class);
    }
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious

The bridge pattern (`@DefaultBean` reactive wrapper delegating to `@DefaultBean` blocking implementation, replaced by `@Alternative` at test time) is a standard Quarkus CDI pattern. Nothing in Quarkus documentation warns that `@DefaultBean` injection points resolve before `@Alternative` activation. The failure is completely silent — no ambiguity error, no warning, just empty results from the no-op. Only `System.identityHashCode()` tracing reveals which implementation was actually injected.

### Why this fix

Solution 1 (bypass the bridge) is preferred because it eliminates the CDI resolution issue entirely and has no test infrastructure side effects. Solution 2 works but creates a maintenance burden — every new alternative added to the memory profile must also be added to every `getEnabledAlternatives()` override.

### Alternatives considered

- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` for the no-op: breaks CDI wiring when the bridge needs a delegate and no alternative is available
- Using `Instance<CbrCaseMemoryStore>` with programmatic lookup: adds complexity without addressing the root cause
- Filing a Quarkus ARC bug: may be working as designed (build-time CDI optimisation)

entries.title: @DefaultBean implementations invisible to CDI when their supertype JAR has no Jandex index
entries.body:
@DefaultBean implementations invisible to CDI when their supertype JAR has no Jandex index

### Symptom

CDI reports "Unsatisfied dependency for type `Foo`" even though:
- A `@ApplicationScoped @DefaultBean` implementation of `Foo` is on the compile classpath
- The implementing JAR contains a valid `META-INF/jandex.idx`
- The implementing class is listed in that index

### Context

A library JAR (`impl-lib`) provides `@DefaultBean class NoOpFoo implements Foo`. A separate JAR (`api-lib`) defines the `Foo` interface. `api-lib` ships without a Jandex index. A downstream module depends on both (directly or transitively).

Quarkus ARC processes the Jandex index of `impl-lib` and finds `NoOpFoo`. When it tries to validate the bean — checking the type hierarchy, qualifiers, and injection points — it needs to read metadata about `Foo` from its defining JAR. Because `api-lib` has no Jandex index, ARC cannot resolve the supertype and silently discards `NoOpFoo` from the CDI graph.

### Root cause

Quarkus ARC bean discovery is index-driven. All types involved in a bean's type hierarchy must be present in **some** Jandex index for the bean to be fully resolved. It is not sufficient for the implementing JAR to have an index — the interface-defining JAR must also be indexed.

### Fix

Add the Jandex plugin to the API JAR's build:

```xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>io.smallrye</groupId>
  <artifactId>jandex-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <id>make-index</id>
      <goals><goal>jandex</goal></goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
```

Or, if you cannot modify the API JAR, force-index it in the consuming module's test config:

```properties
quarkus.index-dependency.my-api.group-id=com.example
quarkus.index-dependency.my-api.artifact-id=my-api
```

Note: `quarkus.index-dependency` is a build-time property and must be set in `application.properties`, not via `QuarkusTestResourceLifecycleManager`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The error message ("Unsatisfied dependency") points at the missing bean, not at the missing index. The implementing class is visually present in the JAR, correctly annotated, and listed in that JAR's Jandex index — all the obvious checks pass. The missing piece is in a completely different JAR.

### Alternative root cause — stale SNAPSHOT cache

The same symptom appears when the API JAR **does** have a Jandex index but the locally cached SNAPSHOT predates the commit that added the new types. This happens when:

1. `api-lib` is updated to add new interface types and a CI run publishes a fresh SNAPSHOT
2. A consuming module refreshes its SNAPSHOT dependency (e.g. `casehub-ledger`) but not `api-lib`
3. The local cache holds an old `api-lib` SNAPSHOT whose index doesn't yet list the new types

**Diagnosis:** check the JAR timestamp in `~/.m2/repository/`. If it's older than the CI run that added the types, refresh:
```bash
mvn install -DskipTests -f ~/path/to/api-lib/pom.xml
```

When refreshing a SNAPSHOT dependency chain (e.g. `casehub-ledger`), always refresh its upstreams (e.g. `casehub-platform`) if the ledger has added dependencies on new platform types.

**See also:** [GE-20260523-afab1d](GE-20260523-afab1d.md) — @ApplicationScoped bean in JAR bytecode invisible to Quarkus ARC without Jandex index | [GE-20260523-20046c](GE-20260523-20046c.md) — %prod.quarkus.index-dependency limits JAR indexing to production

**See also:** [GE-20260609-18a0b1](GE-20260609-18a0b1.md) — quarkus.index-dependency for a JAR with jandex.idx double-scans it (the reverse problem)

**See also:** [GE-20260610-204ddb](GE-20260610-204ddb.md) — stale core module jar breaks CDI resolution — symptom mimics missing @DefaultBean

quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives silently ignores %dev. profile overrides — use exclude-types instead

### Symptom
`%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is set in `application.properties` alongside a non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. In dev mode, the `@Alternative` beans listed in the `%dev.` value are never activated — ArC throws `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for the interfaces they implement, even though the beans exist on the classpath and have Jandex indices.

### Context
Multi-profile Quarkus application needing different CDI alternatives per environment:
- Production: reactive JPA stores (`engine-persistence-hibernate`)
- Dev mode: in-memory blocking stores (`engine-persistence-memory`)
- Tests: separate `application.properties` with its own `selected-alternatives`

Both `%dev.` and non-profiled values present in the same `application.properties`.

### What was tried (didn't work)
1. `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=MemoryPlanItemStore,...` alongside non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=JpaPlanItemStore,...` — dev alternatives silently ignored
2. Removing the non-profiled value and using only `%dev.` and `%prod.` — still ignored
3. Verified `%dev.quarkus.arc.exclude-types` DOES work (OidcCurrentPrincipal successfully excluded in dev) — confirms profile overrides work for other ArC properties

### Root cause
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` is a build-time fixed property that does not honour `%profile.` prefixes. The property is resolved once during Quarkus augmentation and profile-specific values are silently discarded. This is not documented — the Quarkus configuration reference does not distinguish which ArC properties support profile overrides.

### Fix
Select ALL alternatives (both JPA and memory) in the non-profiled `selected-alternatives`. Use profile-specific `exclude-types` to control which survive in each environment:

```properties
# Non-profiled: select everything — both JPA and memory alternatives
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  io.casehub.persistence.jpa.JpaPlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryPlanItemStore,\
  io.casehub.persistence.memory.InMemoryCaseMetaModelRepository

# Dev: exclude reactive JPA stores → memory stores win
%dev.quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.persistence.jpa.JpaPlanItemStore,...

# Prod: exclude memory stores → JPA stores win
%prod.quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.persistence.memory.MemoryPlanItemStore,...
```

ArC processes `exclude-types` first (removing beans entirely), then resolves `selected-alternatives` among surviving beans. In each profile, only one alternative per interface survives — no ambiguity.

### Why this is non-obvious
Profile-specific overrides (`%dev.`, `%prod.`) work for most Quarkus properties, including `quarkus.arc.exclude-types`. The natural assumption is that `selected-alternatives` follows the same pattern. There is no error, warning, or log message when the profile override is ignored — the non-profiled value is silently used. The failure manifests as `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` with no hint about profile resolution.

### Why this fix
`exclude-types` is a coarser mechanism (removes the bean entirely vs just not selecting it), but it's the only ArC property that supports profile overrides. The exclude-types-first-then-resolve pattern is architecturally sound: each profile starts from the same selected set and carves out what doesn't belong.

### Alternatives considered
- **Maven profiles** — add/remove JARs per profile. Rejected: adds build complexity and doesn't work with `quarkus:dev` which uses the default Maven profile.
- **`@IfBuildProfile("dev")` wrapper beans** — create dev-only `@ApplicationScoped` beans that delegate to memory stores. Rejected: code duplication across 5+ SPIs, maintenance burden.
- **Separate `application-dev.properties`** — Quarkus doesn't support this pattern (it's a Spring Boot convention).

entries.title: Static Panache entity calls bypass injected store tenant filtering
Cross-repo SPI extends creates CDI bean displacement — standalone composition required
entries.body:
Cross-repo SPI extends creates CDI bean displacement — standalone composition required

### Symptom
CDI deployment fails with ambiguous bean resolution or unexpected bean displacement when
a neural-text module's `CbrCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore` is on the classpath
alongside platform's `CaseMemoryStore` implementations (JPA, SQLite, inmem).

### Context
`GraphCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore` works within casehub-platform because all
implementations share the same CDI bean archive. Cross-repo, the inheritance creates three
displacement paths:

1. `QdrantCbrCaseMemoryStore` (neural-text, `@ApplicationScoped`) also satisfies
   `CaseMemoryStore` injection points — displaces `JpaMemoryStore` by priority
2. `NoOpCbrCaseMemoryStore` (neural-text, `@DefaultBean`) also becomes a
   `CaseMemoryStore @DefaultBean` — conflicts with `NoOpCaseMemoryStore` (platform)
3. Any `@Alternative` on the subtype cascades to the parent type's injection sites

### Root cause
CDI bean type resolution includes all supertypes. A bean typed as
`CbrCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore` is injectable at both
`@Inject CbrCaseMemoryStore` and `@Inject CaseMemoryStore`. When the SPI
and its extension live in different repos (different CDI archives), the
priority/default-bean resolution rules interact across archive boundaries
in ways that don't occur within a single archive.

### Fix
Make the extended SPI a **standalone interface** — do not extend the base SPI.
Use composition via delegation:

```java
// WRONG — causes displacement
public interface CbrCaseMemoryStore extends CaseMemoryStore { ... }

// RIGHT — standalone SPI, delegates internally
public interface CbrCaseMemoryStore {
    // own methods only — no CaseMemoryStore inheritance
}

// Implementation delegates to injected CaseMemoryStore
@ApplicationScoped
public class QdrantCbrCaseMemoryStore implements CbrCaseMemoryStore {
    @Inject CaseMemoryStore delegate;  // no priority conflict
}
```

### Why this is non-obvious
The `extends` pattern works within a single repo (`GraphCaseMemoryStore extends
CaseMemoryStore` in casehub-platform) because all beans share one CDI archive.
The failure only manifests when the extending SPI lives in a different repo,
which is exactly when composition-over-inheritance is architecturally correct
but not what developers reach for first.

### Alternatives considered
- `@Typed(CbrCaseMemoryStore.class)` annotation to restrict bean types — rejected because it
  must be applied to every implementation, is easy to forget on new implementations, and
  doesn't prevent the `@DefaultBean` dual-registration problem
- Qualifier annotation to distinguish CBR from base memory beans — rejected because it
  changes the injection site contract for all existing `CaseMemoryStore` consumers

entries.title: 'Reactive' Quarkus service classes may use blocking services or Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative in-memory stores don't intercept those paths
entries.body:
'Reactive' Quarkus service classes may use blocking services or Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative in-memory stores don't intercept those paths

### What is undocumented

A service class annotated `@Alternative` and named with "Reactive" may internally use a `blockingService` field (injected blocking CDI service) for write operations and `Entity.find()` (a Panache static) for read operations. CDI `@Alternative @Priority(1)` in-memory stores only intercept at CDI injection points — Panache statics go directly to the underlying database regardless of what alternatives are selected.

### Context

In Quarkus Qhorus (casehubio/qhorus), `ReactiveQhorusMcpTools`:
- `sendMessage()` delegates internally to `blockingMessageService` → `MessageService.send()` → `messageStore.put()` (uses the `MessageStore` CDI alternative, i.e. `InMemoryMessageStore` in tests)
- `getChannelTimeline()` delegates to `blockingGetChannelTimeline()` → `Message.<Message>find(...)` (Panache static — queries H2 directly, bypasses `MessageStore` entirely)

Result: messages written by `sendMessage()` land in `InMemoryMessageStore` (in-memory). Messages read by `getChannelTimeline()` come from H2 (empty in tests). The two paths never share data.

### Discovery

Only visible by reading the service implementation source. The class name and method signatures suggest a uniform reactive abstraction. Not mentioned in any documentation.

### Impact on tests

Tests that call `sendMessage()` then verify the timeline via `getChannelTimeline()` always see an empty timeline in test setups using `@Alternative` in-memory stores, even though the message was "successfully" posted.

### Fix / Workaround

Identify the actual data path for each operation you need to test:
1. Check which CDI service field the MCP tool method delegates to
2. Check whether that service uses CDI store injection or Panache statics
3. For end-to-end write→read tests: use the real H2 database (don't rely on in-memory stores for both sides)

Alternatively, file an upstream issue to make the read path use the same abstraction as the write path.

**See also:** [GE-20260512-66d997](GE-20260512-66d997.md) — Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores

entries.title: Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores — returns empty results silently
entries.body:
Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores — returns empty results silently

## Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores — returns empty results silently

### Symptom

Test suite activates `@Alternative @Priority(1)` InMemory stores via `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives`. Panache static queries (`Entity.<Entity>listAll()`, `Entity.find(...)`) return zero results with no error, even though data was inserted through the store.

### Root cause

Panache static methods resolve directly against JPA at the persistence layer, bypassing CDI entirely. `@Alternative` implementations intercept calls made through injected CDI interfaces, not through static Panache entry points. With InMemory stores active, the JPA entity tables are empty — Panache statics query empty tables and return zero results silently.

### Fix

In test code that activates InMemory stores, never use Panache statics to query domain entities. Always go through the injected store or service layer:

```java
// Wrong — bypasses CDI alternative, queries empty JPA table
List<Channel> channels = Channel.<Channel>listAll();

// Correct — routes through the injected alternative store
List<Channel> channels = channelStore.findAll();
// or via service/tool layer
var result = tools.listChannels();
```

### Why this is non-obvious

Panache statics look like repository methods and feel like they should respect CDI alternatives — but they don't. No error is thrown, no warning is logged; the query simply returns an empty collection. The only signal is silently wrong test data.

**See also:** [GE-20260429-a79d0e](GE-20260429-a79d0e.md) — @Alternative @Priority auto-activates without quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives

**See also:** [GE-20260519-f33c66](GE-20260519-f33c66.md) — 'Reactive' service classes may use Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative doesn't intercept

**See also:** [GE-20260528-3d3847](GE-20260528-3d3847.md) — @Transactional on @BeforeAll static methods has no effect (same CDI proxy limitation)

**See also:** [GE-20260608-d223af](GE-20260608-d223af.md) — REST Assured GPath $.findAll returns null (not []) — Hamcrest not(empty()) silently passes on null

**See also:** [GE-20260609-49bd08](GE-20260609-49bd08.md) — static Panache entity calls bypass injected store tenant filtering

entries.body:
# Module Tier Structure

Three-tier rule for modular library design. Applies to any Quarkus extension or multi-module library.

## The Three Tiers

| Tier | Contents | Dependencies allowed |
|------|----------|---------------------|
| **Tier 1 — Pure-Java SPI** (`api/`) | Interfaces, records, enums, value types | Zero framework deps. CDI annotation JARs (`jakarta.inject-api`, `jakarta.enterprise.cdi-api`) and Mutiny (`io.smallrye.reactive:mutiny` as `provided`) are acceptable — both are inert without a container/runtime and every Quarkus consumer already has them. JPA and Quarkus runtime types remain excluded. |
| **Tier 2 — Core library** (`core/`) | Shared logic, routing strategies, utilities | Tier 1 deps + lightweight libraries. No JPA, no datasource requirements. |
| **Tier 3 — Full extension** (`runtime/`) | CDI beans, JPA entities, Flyway migrations, REST resources | Everything — Quarkus runtime, JPA, datasource config. |

## Rules

**SPI method signatures must not expose heavy external SDK types.** Consumers implement Tier 1 interfaces — their compile classpath should not force vendor SDKs.

**JPA entities must not co-locate with domain SPIs.** Placing entities in the SPI module forces all consumers to configure a datasource. Entities belong in Tier 3 or a dedicated `persistence-*` module.

**Persistence module split.** When a library needs both a domain SPI and a JPA implementation, split them: SPI in Tier 1, JPA impl in a separate `persistence-hibernate/` or `persistence-jpa/` module. Consumers that don't need persistence depend on Tier 1 only.

## SPI Default Patterns

Three patterns for SPI defaults, each with a different rationale:

| Pattern | When to use | Default impl location |
|---------|-------------|----------------------|
| **No-op default** | Operational SPIs where skipping the operation leaves the system functional (`WorkerProvisioner`, `CaseChannelProvider`) | Same pure-Java module as the SPI |
| **Populated default** | Vocabulary/registry SPIs where an empty implementation breaks routing immediately (`CapabilityRegistry`) | Same pure-Java module as the SPI |
| **No-op `@DefaultBean`** | Store SPIs that maintain persistent state (`CaseMemoryStore`, `WorkItemStore`) | Mock module (Tier 3) |

**Anti-pattern:** labelling an `InMemoryXxx` as `@DefaultBean`. `@DefaultBean` means no-op, not in-memory. The in-memory working implementation is `@Alternative @Priority(N)` in a separate `persistence-memory/` module, activated by classpath presence.

## References

- [`persistence-backend-cdi-priority`](persistence-backend-cdi-priority.md) — CDI priority ladder for persistence backends
- [`maven-submodule-folder-naming`](../casehub/maven-submodule-folder-naming.md) — folder naming convention

entries.title: Routing through a gateway method inside @Transactional causes double-persist — split the persistence call from the fan-out
entries.body:
Routing through a gateway method inside @Transactional causes double-persist — split the persistence call from the fan-out

## Symptom

Calling `gateway.post(channelId, message)` inside a `@Transactional` MCP tool method, where `post()` internally calls `agentBackend.post()` → `messageService.send()` (also `@Transactional`), causes a double-persist: the tool method calls `messageService.send()` first for the return value, then `gateway.post()` calls it again through the backend. The message is written twice to the DB.

## Context

Any architecture where a gateway wraps an existing persistence service. The design doc said "route through gateway.post()"; the implementation discovered the double-persist problem when the tool method still needed the `Message` entity returned by `messageService.send()` to build its response.

## Root Cause

The MCP tool method (`@Transactional`) calls `messageService.send()` to get back the persisted entity, then the design required also calling `gateway.post()` which internally calls `messageService.send()` again via `QhorusChannelBackend.post()`. Two writes in the same transaction — same data, same channel.

## Fix

Split the concerns:

1. Keep `messageService.send()` in the tool method — it returns the entity, handles rate limiting, commitment lifecycle, ledger write. This is the source-of-truth write.
2. Add a `gateway.fanOut(UUID channelId, OutboundMessage)` that dispatches **only to external backends** (not the agent backend). Call this after `messageService.send()` returns.
3. Make `gateway.post()` package-private (for unit tests only); document it as a test-only path.

```java
// In sendMessage() @Tool:
Message message = messageService.send(...);              // persistence + ledger
channelGateway.fanOut(channel.id, outboundMessage);      // external backends only
```

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The initial design correctly identified that the gateway should be the single entry point. The transactional trap is invisible until the entity return value forces a direct `messageService.send()` call — at which point the gateway's internal call to the same service becomes redundant. The fix (fanOut vs post) is not obvious because it requires splitting one conceptual operation into two methods with different scope.

entries.title: qhorus persistence-memory module creates three-way CDI ambiguity — reactive wrappers must also be excluded
entries.body:
qhorus persistence-memory module creates three-way CDI ambiguity — reactive wrappers must also be excluded

### Symptom

29 CDI `DeploymentException` errors at Quarkus augmentation time — `Ambiguous dependencies` for every qhorus store type (`InstanceStore`, `ChannelStore`, `MessageStore`, `CommitmentStore`, `DataStore`, `DeliveryCursorStore`, `WatchdogStore`, `ChannelBindingStore`) plus their `@CrossTenant` variants.

### Context

Consumer app (casehub-aml) has three qhorus modules on the classpath:
- `qhorus-runtime` — JPA stores (`io.casehub.qhorus.runtime.store.jpa.*`)
- `qhorus-testing` — in-memory test stores (`io.casehub.qhorus.testing.*`)
- `qhorus-persistence-memory` — standalone in-memory stores (`io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.*`)

All three provide implementations at `@ApplicationScoped @Default` with no `@Alternative` or `@Priority` disambiguation.

### What was tried (didn't work)

1. Rebuilding qhorus locally (`mvn install -DskipTests`) — same result; the ambiguity is in the source, not a bad build artifact.
2. Excluding only the 12 blocking `InMemory*Store` classes from `persistence-memory` — resolves the ambiguity but creates 2 new `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` errors.

### Root cause

The new `qhorus-persistence-memory` module added `InMemory*Store` beans in `io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.*` at `@ApplicationScoped @Default` — same qualifiers as both the JPA stores and the testing module stores. No priority hierarchy was established.

The reactive wrappers (`InMemoryReactiveMessageStore`, `InMemoryReactiveChannelStore`) inject the blocking stores **by concrete type**, not by interface:

```java
// InMemoryReactiveMessageStore
@Inject InMemoryMessageStore blocking;  // concrete type, not MessageStore interface
```

This means excluding the blocking stores without also excluding the reactive wrappers creates `UnsatisfiedResolutionException`.

### Solution 1 — per-class exclude-types

**Approach:** Exclude all persistence-memory stores individually via `quarkus.arc.exclude-types`
**Pros:** No Maven dependency changes; works when persistence-memory is a transitive dep you can't control
**Cons:** Must list every class (14+); must include reactive wrappers too (they inject blocking stores by concrete type); breaks if qhorus-testing also injects persistence-memory classes by concrete type

```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryChannelBindingStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryChannelStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCommitmentStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCrossTenantChannelStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCrossTenantCommitmentStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCrossTenantMessageStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryCrossTenantWatchdogStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryDataStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryDeliveryCursorStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryInstanceStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryMessageStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryWatchdogStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryReactiveMessageStore,\
  io.casehub.qhorus.persistence.memory.InMemoryReactiveChannelStore
```

### Solution 2 — Maven dependency exclusion (recommended)

**Approach:** Exclude `casehub-qhorus-persistence-memory` from the `casehub-qhorus-testing` dependency in the consumer `pom.xml`
**Pros:** One exclusion rule; no `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` needed; eliminates the ambiguity at the dependency level before CDI even sees the beans
**Cons:** Only works when `qhorus-testing` is a direct dependency (not transitive)

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.casehub</groupId>
  <artifactId>casehub-qhorus-testing</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
  <exclusions>
    <exclusion>
      <groupId>io.casehub</groupId>
      <artifactId>casehub-qhorus-persistence-memory</artifactId>
    </exclusion>
  </exclusions>
</dependency>
```

Verified in casehub-life: the testing jar's stores are self-contained — they do not delegate to persistence-memory stores internally. With the exclusion, only the testing jar's `@Alternative @Priority(1)` stores are discovered, and they win over the JPA stores cleanly.

### Why this is non-obvious

The initial symptom (29 ambiguous dependencies) points at the blocking stores. Excluding them seems like the complete fix. But the reactive wrappers have a direct dependency on the concrete blocking store class — not the interface — so excluding the blocking stores creates a new unsatisfied dependency that only surfaces on the next build. Two rounds of "fix one CDI error, get a different one" before reaching the real solution.

### Alternatives considered

- **Rebuilding qhorus** — tried first, doesn't help; the ambiguity is intentional in the source
- **Adding `@Alternative @Priority` to qhorus source** — correct long-term fix but requires a qhorus PR
- **Excluding by package prefix** — Quarkus `exclude-types` doesn't support wildcards; must list each class
