PanacheQuery.stream() does not exist in Quarkus Hibernate Reactive Panache
entries.body:
PanacheQuery.stream() does not exist in Quarkus Hibernate Reactive Panache

## Symptom

Compilation error: `cannot find symbol — method stream()` on a
`io.quarkus.hibernate.reactive.panache.PanacheQuery<T>` instance.

## Context

Trying to implement cursor-backed reactive streaming from a Panache repository,
expecting the same `.stream()` API as the blocking `PanacheQuery<T>` which returns
`Stream<T>`.

## What was tried (didn't work)

```java
return repo.find(jpql, params).stream();  // ← does not compile
```

Inspecting the Panache reactive JAR via `javap` confirms only these methods exist on
`PanacheQuery<T>`: `list()`, `firstResult()`, `singleResult()`, `count()`, `page()`,
`lastPage()`, `hasNextPage()`, `pageCount()`.

## Root cause

The reactive Panache `PanacheQuery<T>` in Quarkus 3.32.x has no `.stream()` method.
Hibernate Reactive does not expose a cursor-backed streaming API in the Panache surface
at this version — only full list materialisation is available.

## Fix

Wrap the materialised list as a `Multi`:

```java
// Still materialises the full list, but gives Multi<T> shape for downstream fold:
return scan(query).toMulti().flatMap(list -> Multi.createFrom().iterable(list));
```

For true cursor-backed streaming, use the native Hibernate Reactive session API
(not Panache) — significantly more complex. Revisit when/if Quarkus exposes
`PanacheQuery.stream()` on the reactive side.

## Why this is non-obvious

The blocking `PanacheQuery<T>` has `.stream()` → `Stream<T>`. Developers familiar with
blocking Panache naturally reach for the same API on the reactive side. The missing method
only surfaces as a compile error with no helpful message pointing at the version gap.

**See also:** [GE-20260602-286f16](GE-20260602-286f16.md) — Mutiny Infrastructure.getDefaultBlockingExecutor() does not exist — use getDefaultExecutor()

**See also:** [GE-20260609-630b35](GE-20260609-630b35.md) — Uni.createFrom().runnable() does not exist

**See also:** [GE-20260617-397d41](GE-20260617-397d41.md) — quarkus-rest-client-reactive does not exist in Quarkus 3.x

entries.title: LedgerAttestation in quarkus-ledger 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT is plain @Entity — Panache statics cause compile error
entries.body:
LedgerAttestation in quarkus-ledger 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT is plain @Entity — Panache statics cause compile error

## Symptom

`AgentMessageLedgerEntryRepository.java` fails to compile with:

```
cannot find symbol: method list(String, UUID)
  location: class io.quarkiverse.ledger.runtime.model.LedgerAttestation
cannot find symbol: method persist()
  location: variable attestation of type LedgerAttestation
```

The error points at your own repository file, not at the quarkus-ledger library. The file's Javadoc comment may say "LedgerAttestation is still a PanacheEntityBase; its Panache static methods are used as-is" — this comment is wrong (or was accurate on an earlier version).

## Root Cause

`LedgerAttestation` in quarkus-ledger 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT is a plain `@Entity` with `@NamedQuery` annotations — it does **not** extend `PanacheEntityBase`. Panache static methods (`list()`, `persist()`, `findById()`, etc.) are not available. The misleading Javadoc is a copy-paste from an earlier design.

## Fix

Replace Panache static calls with `EntityManager` + named queries:

```java
// Instead of: LedgerAttestation.list("ledgerEntryId = ?1 ...", ledgerEntryId)
em.createNamedQuery("LedgerAttestation.findByEntryId", LedgerAttestation.class)
    .setParameter("entryId", ledgerEntryId)
    .getResultList();

// Instead of: attestation.persist()
em.persist(attestation);

// Instead of: LedgerAttestation.list("ledgerEntryId IN ?1", entryIds)
em.createNamedQuery("LedgerAttestation.findByEntryIds", LedgerAttestation.class)
    .setParameter("entryIds", entryIds)
    .getResultList();
```

Named queries are declared as `@NamedQuery` annotations on the `LedgerAttestation` class — check the source jar to find the exact names.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The compile error points at your own code (the repository implementation), not at the library. A developer reading the file would see the Javadoc comment asserting Panache is available and assume the issue is elsewhere. The library API changed from Panache to plain JPA without the consuming code being updated.

**See also:** GE-20260420-7d28fa (PanacheRepository with plain @Entity throws at runtime)

entries.title: GitHub Packages REST API silently truncates org package listing — no pagination indicator
entries.body:
GitHub Packages REST API silently truncates org package listing — no pagination indicator

### Symptom
`gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven'` returns a subset of packages.
Packages known to exist and be published do not appear in the results. No error,
no warning, no indication that results are truncated.

### Context
Auditing whether all Maven modules in a multi-repo build are published to GitHub
Packages. The org has 200+ packages. Default page size is 30.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Single API call to list all packages — returned only ~30, missing entire repos
- Assumed packages were not published and began investigating CI workflows

### Root cause
The GitHub REST API `/orgs/{org}/packages` endpoint paginates at 30 items by
default. Unlike most GitHub API endpoints, the `gh` CLI does not auto-paginate
this one. There is no `total_count` field or obvious truncation marker in the
response — the caller gets a valid JSON array that simply stops early.

### Fix
Use `per_page=100` and iterate pages until an empty page is returned:
```bash
# Page through all packages
gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven&per_page=100&page=1' --jq '.[].name'
gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven&per_page=100&page=2' --jq '.[].name'
# ... until empty result
```

Or check specific packages by name (O(1), no pagination):
```bash
gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages/maven/{groupId}.{artifactId}/versions' \
  --jq '.[0].name' 2>/dev/null || echo "NOT FOUND"
```

### Why this is non-obvious
Most GitHub API endpoints either return all results or include clear pagination
indicators (Link headers, total_count). This endpoint silently returns a partial
list. The natural debugging path is to investigate CI/CD publishing, not API
pagination — especially when the first page contains packages from other repos
in the org, making the response look complete.

### Why this fix
Checking specific packages by name avoids pagination entirely and is O(1) per
package. Use the paginated listing only when you need the full inventory.

entries.title: Testing — Principles
entries.body:
A bug fixed without a test will recur.

---

## Coverage Analysis

**Line coverage is a floor, not a ceiling.** 80% line coverage with no
robustness tests is worse than 60% with comprehensive edge-case coverage.

After writing tests for a feature, explicitly ask:

> "What would have to go wrong in production that my tests would NOT catch?"

Every answer is a missing test.

Keep asking until the answer is "nothing credible."

### Coverage is inadequate when:

- All tests still pass after deleting the function body
- No test triggers any catch block or error handler
- No test asserts a specific return value (only that no exception was thrown)
- Mocks outnumber real I/O calls
- Every test is a unit test with no integration or E2E coverage

### Coverage analysis checklist

Run this after writing tests for any feature:

- [ ] Happy path verified with specific output assertion?
- [ ] Every error branch triggered by at least one test?
- [ ] Boundary values (empty, null, max, min) explicitly tested?
- [ ] Real I/O paths exercised (not only mocked)?
- [ ] Regression test exists if this is a bug fix?
- [ ] Mutation check: if I flip a `>` to `>=`, delete a return statement, or remove a condition — would a test catch it? If not, an assertion is missing.

---

## Test Flakiness Prevention

A flaky test — one that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without code
changes — is worse than no test. It erodes trust in the suite and causes real
failures to be ignored as "probably flaky."

**Apply this section when any of these are present:**

| Trigger | Risk |
|---------|------|
| Async / concurrent code | Race between assertion and completion |
| External services (HTTP, DB, queue) | Timing, network, or ordering variability |
| Date/time dependencies | Results differ by time of day or timezone |
| Shared mutable state between tests | Test-order dependency; passes in isolation, fails in suite |
| Random number generation | Non-deterministic output |
| File system with non-isolated paths | Leftover state from previous run |

**Rules:**
- Never use `sleep()` to wait for async completion — use explicit awaits, callbacks, or polling with a timeout
- Never share mutable state between tests — reset or isolate per test
- Never depend on test execution order — each test must be independent
- Seed or mock random number generators in tests that consume them
- Use injected/fixed clocks for date/time-sensitive logic, never `Date.now()` or `datetime.now()` directly
- Use isolated temp directories per test, never hardcoded paths

**If a test is already flaky:** fix the root cause (race condition, shared state) rather than adding retries. Retries hide the problem; they don't solve it.

---

## High-Value Test Prioritization

Not all tests have equal value. When time is limited:

| Priority | Test type | Reason |
|----------|-----------|--------|
| **1** | E2E for core user flows | High blast radius; catches integration failures invisible to lower layers |
| **2** | Integration tests for I/O paths | Catches wiring bugs; mocks cannot |
| **3** | Robustness / error path tests | Most production bugs are edge cases |
| **4** | Happy path unit tests | Fast feedback for logic-heavy code |
| **5** | Trivial delegation, getters/setters | Skip — near-zero bug-catching value |

Skip Priority 5 entirely. Testing trivial delegation adds maintenance burden
with no meaningful protection.

---

## UI Testing Mandate — Browser Automation Required

**A UI component or page is not tested until a browser has exercised it.**

Visual showcases, static HTML previews, and component demos are documentation,
not tests. They do not verify the feature works. Use Playwright (TypeScript
projects) or the appropriate browser automation tool for the stack.

### Required for any web UI change

At minimum, one browser test covering the happy path:

```typescript
test('user can submit the form', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/the-page');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Success')).toBeVisible();
});
```

### Browser tests must cover

| Scenario | What to assert |
|----------|----------------|
| Happy path | Primary action succeeds; correct UI state appears |
| Validation | Invalid input shows specific error message |
| Async/loading | Loading state visible, then resolved state appears |
| Error state | Server error shows user-facing message, not a crash or blank screen |

### What is NOT acceptable as a UI test

- "Component rendered without throwing" — no behavioral assertion
- A static HTML file opened manually — not a running server, not repeatable
- Screenshots without assertions — documents output, doesn't verify it
- Prose description of manual testing — not automated, not repeatable

If browser automation is not set up in the project, set it up before claiming
any UI work is complete.

---

## Common Pitfalls

| Mistake | Why It's Wrong | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| Mocking all dependencies | Tests verify mock behavior, not real behavior; wiring bugs invisible | Use real implementations for integration tests |
| Testing implementation, not behavior | Tests break on refactor even when behavior unchanged | Assert outcomes, not internal method calls |
| Only happy path tests | Edge cases cause most production bugs | Explicitly write robustness tests per the table above |
| Skipping browser tests for "simple" UI | Browser environment is unpredictable; "simple" still breaks | One Playwright happy path test is mandatory |
| High line coverage = done | Lines ≠ behaviors; error paths often not covered | Run the coverage analysis checklist above |
| Asserting no exception, not correct output | Tests pass even when function returns wrong value | Always assert the specific expected value |

---

## See Also

- `~/.hortora/garden/approaches/code-review.md` — Code review principles (testing section covers TDD enforcement at review time)

entries.title: Testing — Principles
entries.body:
Testing — Principles

# Testing — Principles

**Domain tags:** testing, tdd, coverage, unit-tests, integration-tests, e2e, property-testing, flakiness
**Last reviewed:** 2026-05-29

Universal test strategy foundation. Language-specific skills extend these rules
with framework and tooling specifics.

**Scope:** These principles govern *what kinds* of tests to write and *whether
coverage is adequate*. TDD discipline (red-green-refactor) governs *when* and
*how* to write them — follow both.

---

## Test Taxonomy

Write tests at every layer that provides distinct value. Bias toward tests that
catch real regressions, not tests that inflate a coverage number.

| Layer | What it tests | When to write |
|-------|---------------|---------------|
| **Unit** | Single function/method in isolation | Business logic, algorithms, transformations, validation rules |
| **Integration** | Components working together with real I/O | Repository layers, API handlers, service calls, DB queries |
| **End-to-End** | Complete user journey through real stack | Core user flows — login, checkout, primary feature |
| **UI / Browser** | Real browser against running server | Any web UI change — see UI Testing Mandate below |

### Choosing the right layer

**Write a unit test when:** the code is pure logic with no I/O — algorithms,
transformations, validation, business rules with complex branching. If you can
call the function with plain values and get a plain value back, it's a unit test.

**Write an integration test when:** the code touches real I/O — a database query,
an HTTP call, a file read/write, a message queue. Test with the real thing, not a
mock. If you're tempted to mock the database to write a "unit" test, write an
integration test instead.

**Write an E2E test when:** the feature has a user-visible flow that crosses
multiple layers — HTTP request → service → database → response. Limit to core
flows; not every endpoint needs one.

**Write a browser test (Playwright) when:** the code runs in a browser or renders
HTML — components, pages, forms, interactions. If the output is DOM, test it in a
browser. A TypeScript function with no DOM output does not need Playwright.

One integration test covering a real I/O path is worth more than ten unit tests
mocking the same path. Don't let unit test counts substitute for integration coverage.

---

## What to Write for Every Feature

For each new feature or significant change, cover all four categories. Missing
any of them is incomplete test coverage.

### 1 — Happy Path

The primary success case — the thing users do most often.

- Mandatory for every feature, no exceptions
- Tests what the feature is *for*, not just that it doesn't crash
- Must verify the correct output or state, not just absence of error

### 2 — Correctness

Verify the right answer is produced, not just *an* answer.

- Assert specific return values, state changes, side effects
- `result != null` is not a correctness test — `result == expectedValue` is
- Test each distinct output the function can produce

### 3 — Robustness

Verify the system handles adversarial conditions gracefully.

| Category | Examples |
|----------|----------|
| **Boundary values** | Empty input, max length, zero, negative, off-by-one |
| **Invalid input** | Wrong types, malformed data, missing required fields |
| **Error paths** | Network failure, DB unavailable, timeout, permission denied |
| **Concurrent access** | Duplicate requests, race conditions, stale reads |
| **State edge cases** | Uninitialized, already-deleted entity, partially-complete transaction |

Robustness tests catch most production bugs. Don't skip them because the happy
path passes.

### 4 — Property-Based Testing

**When it applies:** the function has an invariant that should hold for a wide
range of inputs — not just the specific examples you thought of.

Good candidates:
- Algorithms (sort, search, encode/decode, compress/decompress)
- Parsers and serialisers — `deserialise(serialise(x)) == x`
- Mathematical operations — commutativity, associativity, identity
- Data transformations where output properties are knowable from input properties
- Validation functions with large input spaces

**Not applicable for:** UI interactions, simple CRUD, fixed-enum validation,
integration tests, anything where the "correct answer" is defined case-by-case.

Use the appropriate library for the stack (Hypothesis for Python, fast-check for
TypeScript/JavaScript, jqwik for Java). Write properties as invariants, not as
specific input/output pairs:

```python
# ❌ Example-based — only tests what you thought of
assert sorted([3, 1, 2]) == [1, 2, 3]

# ✅ Property-based — holds for any list
@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
def test_sort_is_idempotent(xs):
    assert sorted(sorted(xs)) == sorted(xs)
```

### 5 — Regression Anchors

### ⛔ Bug Fix Workflow — Mandatory

When investigating a bug:

1. **Write a failing test first.** Before touching the fix, write a test that reproduces the problem. Run it and confirm it fails for the right reason.
2. **Apply the fix.** Only after seeing the test fail.
3. **Verify the test passes.** Run the test again. It must go green.
4. **Verify no regressions.** Run the full test suite.
5. **Report back only after step 4 passes.** Never claim a fix is complete until the tests confirm it.

A test written after the fix can pass for the wrong reasons. The failing test is the evidence that the fix addresses the actual bug, not a coincidental symptom. A bug fixed without a test will recur.

---

## Coverage Analysis

**Line coverage is a floor, not a ceiling.** 80% line coverage with no
robustness tests is worse than 60% with comprehensive edge-case coverage.

After writing tests for a feature, explicitly ask:

> "What would have to go wrong in production that my tests would NOT catch?"

Every answer is a missing test. Keep asking until the answer is "nothing credible."

### Coverage is inadequate when:

entries.title: TDD for constant renames — write a PASS test first to pin existing behaviour
entries.body:
TDD for constant renames — write a PASS test first to pin existing behaviour

# TDD for constant renames — write a PASS test first to pin existing behaviour

## Why this is non-obvious

Standard TDD pedagogy is **RED-GREEN-REFACTOR**: write a failing test, make it pass, then refactor. For a constant rename (e.g. `MAX_PROVIDER` → `MAX_MODEL_IDENTIFIER`), this pattern inverts. The natural instinct is to write the test *after* the rename and call sites are updated. But that loses critical evidence: you can no longer distinguish "this test passes because the boundary is correct" from "this test passes because I made a mistake and the compiler accepted it anyway."

The GREEN-first run is a **characterisation test** — it proves the test is meaningful without requiring an intentional failure state.

## The sequence

1. Write the boundary test (e.g. `modelFamily_exceeds_200_chars_throws`)
2. Run it — expect **GREEN** (the bound already applies via the old constant)
3. Add the new correctly-named constant (alongside the old one)
4. Update all call sites to the new name
5. Run again — still **GREEN**

The pre-rename GREEN run is your evidence that the test would fail if the constant were wrong.

## Constraints

Applies to any constant rename, especially constants that encode business rules or limits. Most valuable when the constant encodes a boundary condition or validation rule.

## Alternatives considered

- **Rename without testing first:** Faster initially, but loses the safety net. If you mistype the constant name or the value, you won't know.
- **Write the test after the rename:** Functionally equivalent for a passing test, but you lose the pre-rename baseline. If the test fails later, was the bound wrong originally or did you change it?

## Why this fix

The evidence is the fix. The pre-rename GREEN run proves your test is sensitive to the constant's actual value. Without it, you're working blind on refactoring work.

## Context

Applied during [eidos#24](https://github.com/casehubio/eidos/issues/24) for `MAX_MODEL_IDENTIFIER` and `MAX_DATA_HANDLING_POLICY` constant renames in `AgentDescriptorValidator`.

entries.title: IntelliJ ide_refactor_rename with relatedRenamingStrategy:none renames one overload precisely — declaration and internal call sites updated, sibling overloads untouched
entries.body:
IntelliJ ide_refactor_rename with relatedRenamingStrategy:none renames one overload precisely — declaration and internal call sites updated, sibling overloads untouched

## IntelliJ ide_refactor_rename with relatedRenamingStrategy:none renames one overload precisely — declaration and internal call sites updated, sibling overloads untouched

### Context

A Java class has multiple public methods with the same name — one annotated with `@Tool` and a
testability overload without. Goal: rename only the testability overload (4-param) without touching
the `@Tool` version (3-param), while still having IntelliJ update all call sites for the renamed
overload.

### Technique

Use `ide_refactor_rename` with `overrideStrategy: rename_only_current` and
`relatedRenamingStrategy: none`, targeting the specific overload by line/column:

```json
{
  "file": "runtime/src/main/java/.../QhorusMcpTools.java",
  "line": 930,
  "column": 24,
  "newName": "requestApprovalWithCorrelationId",
  "overrideStrategy": "rename_only_current",
  "relatedRenamingStrategy": "none"
}
```

Result: IntelliJ renamed the 4-param method declaration AND all call sites of that specific overload
(including internal call sites within the same file), while leaving the 3-param `@Tool` method
completely untouched. `changesCount: 1` referred to files changed, not individual rename occurrences.

### Why this is non-obvious

The natural approach when renaming one overload of many is text-based find-and-replace scoped to
the exact signature — fragile, misses internal call sites, and doesn't update references in other
files. IntelliJ's semantic rename naturally wants to rename ALL overloads together or none. The
`overrideStrategy` + `relatedRenamingStrategy` combination threads the needle: semantic accuracy
for the target overload, surgical non-involvement for the others. The parameters are documented in
the MCP tool schema but the combination for targeted overload rename is not explicitly described.

### When to apply

When a class has multiple overloads of the same method and you need to rename exactly one to
eliminate a naming conflict (e.g. a convenience overload that shadows a `@Tool`-annotated method
from a framework scanner) while all other overloads keep their names.

Fixing a shared resolution method misses non-focal rendering paths
entries.body:
Fixing a shared resolution method misses non-focal rendering paths

## Symptom

A resolution method fix is applied to two of three rendering paths that call it. The third path silently continues using the old (broken) resolution — no compile error, no test failure if the affected code path isn't specifically tested.

## Context

In `EidosRenderPipeline`, `vocabUriForSlot()` was added to fix a `domainVocabulary` fallback gap. It was applied to:
- `buildDescriptorPayload()` — the LLM payload path (actively being modified this session)
- `assembleA2aCard()` — the feature under development (where the change originated)
- ❌ missed: `assembleMarkdownStructural()` — the structural renderer (not in focus)

An agent configured with only `domainVocabulary` got correct slot vocabulary context in two render formats but raw slot string in structural markdown. No test covered this combination.

## Root cause

Developers naturally fix the rendering paths they are actively looking at. The mental model is "I fixed the resolution method and its callers" — but in practice "callers" means "the callers I examined during this change", not "all callers of the old access pattern".

The structural renderer was in a separate method not part of the feature being built, so it was not in the developer's attention window during the fix.

## Fix

Before completing any fix to a shared resolution method, find all callers of the old access pattern — not just the method you changed:

```
IntelliJ: Find Usages on the old access pattern
          (e.g. the field access `descriptor.slotVocabulary()` that the new method replaces)
```

In this case: searching for `slotVocabulary()` across `EidosRenderPipeline` revealed `assembleMarkdownStructural()` as the third caller. All callers need the updated resolution.

The code reviewer who catches this will frame it as "the spec said fix both X and Y, but Z was also there." The implementer will not have noticed Z because Z was not their focus.

## Why this is non-obvious

The fix feels complete because it works on the paths you tested. Multi-renderer systems have a structural property that makes this systematically dangerous: each renderer reads the same model but lives in a separate method. There is no compile-time signal that a third renderer was missed — the old code still compiles, and it still runs correctly for agents that have the specific vocabulary field set explicitly. Only agents using the fallback path expose the gap, and only if structural markdown is the tested format.

entries.title: Routing through a gateway method inside @Transactional causes double-persist — split the persistence call from the fan-out
entries.body:
Routing through a gateway method inside @Transactional causes double-persist — split the persistence call from the fan-out

## Symptom

Calling `gateway.post(channelId, message)` inside a `@Transactional` MCP tool method, where `post()` internally calls `agentBackend.post()` → `messageService.send()` (also `@Transactional`), causes a double-persist: the tool method calls `messageService.send()` first for the return value, then `gateway.post()` calls it again through the backend. The message is written twice to the DB.

## Context

Any architecture where a gateway wraps an existing persistence service. The design doc said "route through gateway.post()"; the implementation discovered the double-persist problem when the tool method still needed the `Message` entity returned by `messageService.send()` to build its response.

## Root Cause

The MCP tool method (`@Transactional`) calls `messageService.send()` to get back the persisted entity, then the design required also calling `gateway.post()` which internally calls `messageService.send()` again via `QhorusChannelBackend.post()`. Two writes in the same transaction — same data, same channel.

## Fix

Split the concerns:

1. Keep `messageService.send()` in the tool method — it returns the entity, handles rate limiting, commitment lifecycle, ledger write. This is the source-of-truth write.
2. Add a `gateway.fanOut(UUID channelId, OutboundMessage)` that dispatches **only to external backends** (not the agent backend). Call this after `messageService.send()` returns.
3. Make `gateway.post()` package-private (for unit tests only); document it as a test-only path.

```java
// In sendMessage() @Tool:
Message message = messageService.send(...);              // persistence + ledger
channelGateway.fanOut(channel.id, outboundMessage);      // external backends only
```

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

The initial design correctly identified that the gateway should be the single entry point. The transactional trap is invisible until the entity return value forces a direct `messageService.send()` call — at which point the gateway's internal call to the same service becomes redundant. The fix (fanOut vs post) is not obvious because it requires splitting one conceptual operation into two methods with different scope.

entries.title: 'Reactive' Quarkus service classes may use blocking services or Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative in-memory stores don't intercept those paths
entries.body:
'Reactive' Quarkus service classes may use blocking services or Panache statics internally — CDI @Alternative in-memory stores don't intercept those paths

### What is undocumented

A service class annotated `@Alternative` and named with "Reactive" may internally use a `blockingService` field (injected blocking CDI service) for write operations and `Entity.find()` (a Panache static) for read operations. CDI `@Alternative @Priority(1)` in-memory stores only intercept at CDI injection points — Panache statics go directly to the underlying database regardless of what alternatives are selected.

### Context

In Quarkus Qhorus (casehubio/qhorus), `ReactiveQhorusMcpTools`:
- `sendMessage()` delegates internally to `blockingMessageService` → `MessageService.send()` → `messageStore.put()` (uses the `MessageStore` CDI alternative, i.e. `InMemoryMessageStore` in tests)
- `getChannelTimeline()` delegates to `blockingGetChannelTimeline()` → `Message.<Message>find(...)` (Panache static — queries H2 directly, bypasses `MessageStore` entirely)

Result: messages written by `sendMessage()` land in `InMemoryMessageStore` (in-memory). Messages read by `getChannelTimeline()` come from H2 (empty in tests). The two paths never share data.

### Discovery

Only visible by reading the service implementation source. The class name and method signatures suggest a uniform reactive abstraction. Not mentioned in any documentation.

### Impact on tests

Tests that call `sendMessage()` then verify the timeline via `getChannelTimeline()` always see an empty timeline in test setups using `@Alternative` in-memory stores, even though the message was "successfully" posted.

### Fix / Workaround

Identify the actual data path for each operation you need to test:
1. Check which CDI service field the MCP tool method delegates to
2. Check whether that service uses CDI store injection or Panache statics
3. For end-to-end write→read tests: use the real H2 database (don't rely on in-memory stores for both sides)

Alternatively, file an upstream issue to make the read path use the same abstraction as the write path.

**See also:** [GE-20260512-66d997](GE-20260512-66d997.md) — Panache static methods bypass CDI @Alternative stores

entries.title: GitHub Packages REST API silently truncates org package listing — no pagination indicator
entries.body:
GitHub Packages REST API silently truncates org package listing — no pagination indicator

### Symptom
`gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven'` returns a subset of packages.
Packages known to exist and be published do not appear in the results. No error,
no warning, no indication that results are truncated.

### Context
Auditing whether all Maven modules in a multi-repo build are published to GitHub
Packages. The org has 200+ packages. Default page size is 30.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Single API call to list all packages — returned only ~30, missing entire repos
- Assumed packages were not published and began investigating CI workflows

### Root cause
The GitHub REST API `/orgs/{org}/packages` endpoint paginates at 30 items by
default. Unlike most GitHub API endpoints, the `gh` CLI does not auto-paginate
this one. There is no `total_count` field or obvious truncation marker in the
response — the caller gets a valid JSON array that simply stops early.

### Fix
Use `per_page=100` and iterate pages until an empty page is returned:
```bash
# Page through all packages
gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven&per_page=100&page=1' --jq '.[].name'
gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages?package_type=maven&per_page=100&page=2' --jq '.[].name'
# ... until empty result
```

Or check specific packages by name (O(1), no pagination):
```bash
gh api 'orgs/{org}/packages/maven/{groupId}.{artifactId}/versions' \
  --jq '.[0].name' 2>/dev/null || echo "NOT FOUND"
```

### Why this is non-obvious
Most GitHub API endpoints either return all results or include clear pagination
indicators (Link headers, total_count). This endpoint silently returns a partial
list. The natural debugging path is to investigate CI/CD publishing, not API
pagination — especially when the first page contains packages from other repos
in the org, making the response look complete.

### Why this fix
Checking specific packages by name avoids pagination entirely and is O(1) per
package. Use the paginated listing only when you need the full inventory.

entries.title: quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size controls tools/list pagination — undocumented default of 50 silently truncates large tool sets
entries.body:
quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size controls tools/list pagination — undocumented default of 50 silently truncates large tool sets

## `quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size` controls tools/list pagination — undocumented default of 50 silently truncates large tool sets

### Stack
quarkus-mcp-server 1.11.1 (Quarkiverse)

### What it is
`quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size` is a runtime configuration property in quarkus-mcp-server that controls how many tools are returned per `tools/list` MCP response. It is defined in `McpServerRuntimeConfig.java` as a nested interface:

```java
public interface Tools {
    @WithDefault("50")
    int pageSize();
    // ...
}
```

### How to use it

**Disable pagination** (return all tools in one response):
```properties
quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size=0
```

**Set a custom page size:**
```properties
quarkus.mcp.server.tools.page-size=100
```

Setting to 0 or any negative number disables pagination entirely — all registered tools are returned in a single `tools/list` response regardless of count.

### Where it's not documented
As of quarkus-mcp-server 1.11.1, this property does not appear in the main Quarkiverse documentation for the extension. It is only discoverable by:
- Reading the `McpServerRuntimeConfig.java` source
- Noticing that `tools/list` returns fewer tools than expected (no warning is emitted)
- Decompiling the deployment JAR

### Discovery path
Found by: diagnosing silent tool truncation (49 Qhorus + 8 Claudony = 57 total tools, response showing exactly 50 alphabetically-sorted tools). Traced through `ToolMessageHandler` → `fetchPage()` → `serverConfig.tools().pageSize()` → `@WithDefault("50")` in `McpServerRuntimeConfig`.

### Related config
The same nested config likely controls pagination for other MCP feature types (prompts, resources) via similar `pageSize()` methods. The naming convention is `quarkus.mcp.server.<feature-type>.page-size`.

**See also:** GE-20260501-50a9f4 — quarkus-mcp-server silently caps tools/list at 50 | GE-20260414-fa6489 — @ToolArg undocumented required and defaultValue attributes

entries.title: Removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation CDI chain silently changes resolution — no AmbiguousResolutionException
entries.body:
Removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation CDI chain silently changes resolution — no AmbiguousResolutionException

### Symptom

After removing `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from one CDI bean, a different bean
silently becomes the active implementation. No `AmbiguousResolutionException`, no
warning, no log. Tests that depend on the removed bean's behaviour fail with
unrelated-looking assertion errors.

### Context

Three implementations of the same port interface coexist in the build:

| Bean | Annotations | Role |
|------|------------|------|
| `PrReviewService` | `@ApplicationScoped @DefaultBean` | Layer 1 naive baseline |
| `QhorusPrReviewService` | `@ApplicationScoped @Alternative @Priority(1)` | Layer 3 qhorus messaging |
| `PrReviewCaseService` | `@ApplicationScoped @Alternative @Priority(2)` | Layer 5 engine (active) |

This is the CDI displacement pattern for progressive layer integration — each layer
adds an implementation; CDI priority determines which is active at runtime.

### What was tried (didn't work)

Removed `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from `PrReviewCaseService` to fix an anti-pattern
documented in ARC42STORIES §8 ("CDI priority gymnastics"). Expected: the plain
`@ApplicationScoped` bean would still displace the `@DefaultBean` baseline via
Quarkus's `@DefaultBean` semantics.

### Root cause

CDI resolution rules interact in a non-obvious way:

1. `@DefaultBean` beans are suppressed when any non-`@DefaultBean` bean exists ✅
2. Activated `@Alternative` beans (with `@Priority`) take precedence over regular beans ⚠️
3. After removing `@Alternative` from `PrReviewCaseService`, it becomes a regular bean
4. `QhorusPrReviewService` (`@Alternative @Priority(1)`) is still an activated alternative
5. **Rule 2 applies**: the activated alternative wins over the regular bean
6. `QhorusPrReviewService` becomes the active implementation — silently

The mental model "I'm just removing unnecessary annotations" is wrong. The annotations
are load-bearing: they participate in a priority chain where every bean's annotation
set matters.

### Fix

All implementations in the `@Alternative` chain must be addressed together, not one at
a time. To properly fix the anti-pattern:

- Either make ALL non-baseline implementations use `@DefaultBean` displacement
  (remove `@Alternative @Priority` from all of them and ensure only one non-`@DefaultBean` exists)
- Or keep the `@Alternative @Priority` chain intact and accept it as the mechanism
  for layer coexistence

Do not remove `@Alternative` from one bean without checking what other `@Alternative`
implementations exist for the same interface.

### Why this is non-obvious

Most developers reason about CDI alternatives in pairs: "my bean vs the default."
The three-way interaction (DefaultBean + Alternative(1) + Alternative(2)) is rarely
encountered, and the silent resolution change (no exception, wrong bean) gives no
diagnostic signal. The symptom (test assertion failure on unrelated data) is
completely disconnected from the cause (CDI annotation change).

### Why this fix

The obvious approach — "just remove the anti-pattern annotation" — is wrong because
it treats the annotations as decoration rather than as a load-bearing priority chain.
The fix requires understanding the full set of implementations and their annotation
interactions before changing any single one.

### Alternatives considered

- Remove `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from only the active bean → silently breaks resolution (this gotcha)
- Remove `@Alternative` from ALL implementations and use `@DefaultBean` displacement → requires ensuring exactly one non-`@DefaultBean` impl, and retiring or `@DefaultBean`-ing the intermediate layers
- Keep `@Alternative @Priority` chain as-is → accepted as the working mechanism until a coordinated cleanup addresses all implementations together

**See also:** GE-20260626-c21b02 — @DefaultBean suppression by any Instance<T> peer, a different silent failure in the same CDI displacement space.

entries.title: Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied
entries.body:
Two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → Quarkus AmbiguousResolutionException, not Unsatisfied

## What happened

Two `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` implementations of the same SPI type appeared on the CDI
classpath simultaneously (one from a platform mock library, one from a persistence testing module).
Quarkus reported **"Ambiguous dependencies"** and refused to start — even though both beans
explicitly said "I am a default, defer to anyone else".

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is documented as "yield to any other bean of the same type". With two
`@DefaultBean` beans and no non-default implementation, neither bean yields — the contract
("yield to someone else") cannot resolve because there IS no "someone else" with higher
precedence. The error message is **Ambiguous** (same as two regular `@ApplicationScoped`
beans conflicting), not **Unsatisfied** (what you'd expect if both were supposedly yielding).
Developers often assume two `@DefaultBean` beans resolve cleanly because they both "opt in"
to being overridden.

## Root cause

CDI/ARC `@DefaultBean` semantics: a default bean is only eligible when no other bean at
the same or higher priority is eligible. With two `@DefaultBean` beans and no higher-priority
bean, the tie-break is undefined — ARC treats this as an ambiguous injection point.

## Fix

Exclude the unwanted `@DefaultBean` implementation via `application.properties`:
```properties
quarkus.arc.exclude-types=io.casehub.platform.mock.MockCurrentPrincipal,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockGroupMembershipProvider,\
  io.casehub.platform.mock.MockPreferenceProvider
```

This removes the conflicting bean from CDI discovery entirely, leaving the desired
`@DefaultBean` as the sole implementation. Prefer excluding the one that returns null or
uninitialized values rather than the one with correct sentinel behaviour.

### Why this fix

`@Alternative @Priority(N)` would also work, but requires activating it via
`selected-alternatives` — that is a heavier configuration change and makes the
intent less clear. `exclude-types` is surgical: "this specific class should not
participate in CDI at all in this context."

### Alternative — use `Instance<T>` with `isUnsatisfied()` to avoid the conflict entirely

Rather than excluding a conflicting bean after the fact, don't provide a competing `@DefaultBean` in the extension at all. Inject `Instance<T>` and check `isUnsatisfied()` at call time:

```java
@Inject Instance<PreferenceProvider> preferenceProviderInstance;

int threshold;
if (preferenceProviderInstance.isUnsatisfied()) {
    threshold = DEFAULT_VALUE;  // no provider on classpath
} else {
    threshold = preferenceProviderInstance.get().resolve(...).getOrDefault(KEY).value();
}
```

`Instance<T>` always satisfies its own injection point (the container injects the `Instance` holder, not `T` directly). When zero beans of type `T` exist, `isUnsatisfied()` returns `true`; when one is active, `.get()` returns it. No `@DefaultBean` is added to the extension, so no conflict can arise.

**Best for:** library/extension authors who control their own code and want to make a platform SPI optional without contributing a competing `@DefaultBean`.

**Limitation:** requires call-site guards (`isUnsatisfied()` before `.get()`); callers that inject `T` directly still get an ambiguous point if two `@DefaultBean` beans exist from other sources.

## Constraints

Applies when both `@DefaultBean` implementations reach the CDI container's scanning phase
(i.e. both are indexed via `quarkus.index-dependency` or are in the app's own sources).
In two-repo / multi-module projects, platform library JARs can silently contribute
`@DefaultBean` mocks that conflict with internal no-ops.

## Alternatives considered

- Mark one bean `@Alternative @Priority(1)` instead of `@DefaultBean` — works but changes
  the semantics of the "winning" bean and requires `selected-alternatives` configuration.
- Remove one of the `@DefaultBean` implementations from the classpath entirely — clean, but
  may not be possible if it comes from a third-party dependency.

## Invalidation triggers

Would change if Quarkus ARC adds a deterministic tie-break for two `@DefaultBean` beans
(e.g. favour the one in the current module's sources). Track Quarkus changelog for ARC
`@DefaultBean` resolution changes.

**See also:** [GE-20260515-fd3156](GE-20260515-fd3156.md) — @DefaultBean must be on @Produces method not on the class | [GE-20260529-ab148d](GE-20260529-ab148d.md) — multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException | [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex-indexed JARs

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean

**See also:** [GE-20260609-26ffa5](GE-20260609-26ffa5.md) — @ApplicationScoped POJO + @Produces for same type causes CDI ambiguous bean resolution

**See also:** [GE-20260515-99cf39](GE-20260515-99cf39.md) — config-driven @Produces @DefaultBean for engine-internal strategy selection

**See also:** [GE-20260614-337397](GE-20260614-337397.md) — quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel, clashing with @DefaultBean fallback | [GE-20260604-b3d2ef](GE-20260604-b3d2ef.md) — quarkus-flow CDI extension already registers WorkflowApplication — adding @Produces causes ambiguity

**See also:** [GE-20260615-6c4767](../casehub-engine/GE-20260615-6c4767.md) — adding custom CDI qualifier to @ApplicationScoped removes @Default

**See also:** GE-20260627-51e402 — @Alternative totally suppresses @DefaultBean (not just deprioritized, gone from container)

entries.title: @Alternative on a CDI bean silently suppresses all @DefaultBean beans of the same type — they vanish from the container entirely
Resolve CDI ambiguity between two competing @DefaultBean implementations by introducing a concrete non-default bean
entries.body:
Resolve CDI ambiguity between two competing @DefaultBean implementations by introducing a concrete non-default bean

## Context

Two `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` beans from different JARs both implement the same interface. CDI can't resolve which to use and throws `AmbiguousResolutionException`. Standard approaches don't help:

- `quarkus.arc.exclude-types` is silently ignored for beans from Jandex-indexed JARs (see GE-20260601-848232)
- Marking one as `@Alternative` requires changes to a JAR you don't own
- `@Priority` on `@Alternative` has CDI 2.0 global-scope problems

## Technique

Add a concrete `@ApplicationScoped` bean to your project (production or test sources as appropriate) that implements the conflicting interface:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
public class ProjectGroupMembershipProvider implements GroupMembershipProvider {
    @Override
    public Set<GroupMember> membersOf(String groupName) {
        return Set.of(); // or delegate to preferred implementation
    }
}
```

CDI selects the most-specific non-default bean. Since your bean is NOT `@DefaultBean`, it wins over both competing `@DefaultBean` implementations and the `AmbiguousResolutionException` is resolved. No changes to any JAR required.

## Why This Is Non-Obvious

Most developers reach for `exclude-types` first (fails silently for Jandex-indexed JARs), then try `@Priority` on one of the `@DefaultBean` beans (requires modifying third-party JARs), then consider `@Alternative` + `selected-alternatives` (same problem). The CDI suppression rule — "a non-default bean beats all @DefaultBean candidates for the same type" — is the correct lever, and a thin adapter class is the minimal mechanism that activates it without touching any dependency.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex JARs | [GE-20260601-3dbc80](GE-20260601-3dbc80.md) — exclude-types as technique for @DefaultBean ambiguity

**See also:** [GE-20260601-7a3b38](GE-20260601-7a3b38.md) — @DefaultBean invisible when supertype JAR has no Jandex index

**See also:** [GE-20260616-d70e7e](GE-20260616-d70e7e.md) — selected-alternatives silently accepts non-@Alternative beans

entries.title: @DefaultBean silently suppressed by any Instance<T> peer — breaks multi-implementation SPI patterns
entries.body:
@DefaultBean silently suppressed by any Instance<T> peer — breaks multi-implementation SPI patterns

### Symptom
Agent drift checking silently stops working after adding `@DefaultBean` to `AgentDriftChecker` — no error, no warning. The bean is never injected.

### Context
`DeploymentActualStateAdapter` injects `Instance<NodeDriftChecker>` and builds a `Map<String, NodeDriftChecker>` keyed by `nodeType()`. Four implementations exist: `AgentDriftChecker`, `ChannelDriftChecker`, `CaseTypeDriftChecker`, `TrustPolicyDriftChecker`. Each serves a different `nodeType()` but all implement `NodeDriftChecker`.

The goal was to make `AgentDriftChecker` replaceable by a richer implementation via classpath presence — the standard `@DefaultBean` → `@Alternative @Priority(1)` pattern used successfully elsewhere (e.g. `NoOpAgentStateStore` → `InMemoryAgentStateStore`).

### Root cause
Quarkus `@DefaultBean` suppression operates on **bean types** (interface types), not concrete classes. When `AgentDriftChecker` is `@DefaultBean` and `ChannelDriftChecker` (also implementing `NodeDriftChecker`) is `@ApplicationScoped`, ArC sees a non-default bean with the same interface type and suppresses the `@DefaultBean` — regardless of the fact that they serve completely different runtime roles via `nodeType()`.

The `@DefaultBean` pattern is designed for **single-injection-point replacement**: one interface, one default, one override. It is incompatible with `Instance<T>` multi-bean collection where implementations are distinguished by a runtime discriminator.

### What was tried (didn't work)
1. `@DefaultBean` on `AgentDriftChecker` — suppressed by `ChannelDriftChecker` existing
2. `@Alternative @Priority(1)` on the replacement — both beans appear in `Instance<T>` iteration, `HashMap.put()` non-deterministic winner for the same `nodeType()` key

### Fix
Do not use `@DefaultBean` or `@Alternative` for multi-implementation SPI patterns collected via `Instance<T>`. Instead, either:
- Enrich the existing bean directly (no displacement needed)
- Add priority-aware resolution in the adapter: `checkers.merge(nodeType, checker, (existing, incoming) -> getPriority(incoming) > getPriority(existing) ? incoming : existing)`

### Why this is non-obvious
The `@DefaultBean` pattern works flawlessly for single-injection patterns throughout the codebase (6+ SPIs use it). The mental model — "default vanishes when a better one arrives" — is correct for that context. The failure mode here is that *any* `NodeDriftChecker` implementation (not just an agent-specific one) triggers suppression. No error, no warning, no log. The bean simply disappears from the `Instance<T>` iteration.

### Why this fix
Enriching the existing bean avoids all CDI displacement complexity. The comparison logic (pure Java utility) lives in the type-owning module; the SPI implementation stays in the consumer module unchanged. No CDI annotations change, no new beans, no Instance<T> interaction to reason about.

### Alternatives considered
- Priority-aware adapter resolution — works but adds complexity to the adapter for a problem that only exists because of the displacement pattern
- Bridge module with `@Alternative @Priority(1)` — both beans appear in Instance iteration; HashMap collision is non-deterministic
- Composition approach (AgentNodeSpec wrapping AgentDescriptor) — blocked by tenancyId being required in AgentDescriptor's compact constructor

**See also:** GE-20260623-c651a1 — removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation chain silently changes resolution, another CDI displacement gotcha.

@IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs
entries.body:
@IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs

### Symptom

Adding a dev-profile-only CDI bean (e.g., a `CurrentPrincipal` for dev mode) via `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` causes startup failures — all beans from the non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` list disappear.

### Context

Quarkus profile-specific properties (`%dev.`, `%test.`, `%prod.`) completely **replace** their non-profiled counterparts. If the base `application.properties` has:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  com.example.JpaRepo,\
  com.example.JpaPlanItemStore,\
  com.example.JpaSubCaseGroupRepo
```

Adding `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` drops all three JPA alternatives in dev mode — CDI startup fails with unsatisfied dependency errors for every bean that was in the original list.

### Root cause

Profile-specific properties in Quarkus are full replacements, not merges. This is by design (SmallRye Config behaviour), but the failure mode is silent — no warning that the non-profiled value was dropped.

### Fix

Use bean-level annotations instead of `selected-alternatives`:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
@Priority(150)  // beats OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)
@IfBuildProfile("dev")
public class DemoCurrentPrincipal implements CurrentPrincipal {
    @Override public String tenancyId() { return "demo-tenant"; }
    @Override public String actorId()   { return "demo-user"; }
}
```

**Requirements:**
1. The bean must live in a **Jandex-indexed JAR** (e.g., the application's own `runtime/` module). ArC discovers it automatically — no `selected-alternatives` entry needed.
2. `@IfBuildProfile("dev")` excludes the bean entirely from non-dev builds — no ambiguity in production.
3. `@Priority(150)` resolves over competing `@Alternative` beans (e.g., `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)`) via standard ArC priority resolution.

This is the same mechanism by which `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Alternative @Priority(100)` beats `MockCurrentPrincipal @DefaultBean` in production — without being listed in `selected-alternatives`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The natural instinct is `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=MyDevBean` — it looks like the standard profile-override pattern. The replacement behaviour is documented for SmallRye Config but not prominently flagged in the Quarkus CDI guide. The failure (dropped JPA alternatives) manifests as unrelated `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` errors that don't mention `selected-alternatives` at all.

### Why this fix

`@IfBuildProfile + @Priority` solves the problem at the bean level — no configuration property needed. The alternative (duplicating the full `selected-alternatives` list in every profile override) is fragile and drifts as new alternatives are added.

### Alternatives considered

- **Duplicate the full list in `%dev.`** — works but fragile; every new `@Alternative` bean must be added to every profile-specific override. Drifts silently.
- **Use `@UnlessBuildProfile("prod")` instead of `@IfBuildProfile("dev")`** — activates in both dev and test profiles, which may not be desired. Test profile has its own `FixedCurrentPrincipal @Priority(200)`.

entries.title: @Produces @DefaultBean for library-level overridable CDI defaults without @Alternative
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

entries.title: Removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation CDI chain silently changes resolution — no AmbiguousResolutionException
entries.body:
Removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation CDI chain silently changes resolution — no AmbiguousResolutionException

### Symptom

After removing `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from one CDI bean, a different bean
silently becomes the active implementation. No `AmbiguousResolutionException`, no
warning, no log. Tests that depend on the removed bean's behaviour fail with
unrelated-looking assertion errors.

### Context

Three implementations of the same port interface coexist in the build:

| Bean | Annotations | Role |
|------|------------|------|
| `PrReviewService` | `@ApplicationScoped @DefaultBean` | Layer 1 naive baseline |
| `QhorusPrReviewService` | `@ApplicationScoped @Alternative @Priority(1)` | Layer 3 qhorus messaging |
| `PrReviewCaseService` | `@ApplicationScoped @Alternative @Priority(2)` | Layer 5 engine (active) |

This is the CDI displacement pattern for progressive layer integration — each layer
adds an implementation; CDI priority determines which is active at runtime.

### What was tried (didn't work)

Removed `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from `PrReviewCaseService` to fix an anti-pattern
documented in ARC42STORIES §8 ("CDI priority gymnastics"). Expected: the plain
`@ApplicationScoped` bean would still displace the `@DefaultBean` baseline via
Quarkus's `@DefaultBean` semantics.

### Root cause

CDI resolution rules interact in a non-obvious way:

1. `@DefaultBean` beans are suppressed when any non-`@DefaultBean` bean exists ✅
2. Activated `@Alternative` beans (with `@Priority`) take precedence over regular beans ⚠️
3. After removing `@Alternative` from `PrReviewCaseService`, it becomes a regular bean
4. `QhorusPrReviewService` (`@Alternative @Priority(1)`) is still an activated alternative
5. **Rule 2 applies**: the activated alternative wins over the regular bean
6. `QhorusPrReviewService` becomes the active implementation — silently

The mental model "I'm just removing unnecessary annotations" is wrong. The annotations
are load-bearing: they participate in a priority chain where every bean's annotation
set matters.

### Fix

All implementations in the `@Alternative` chain must be addressed together, not one at
a time. To properly fix the anti-pattern:

- Either make ALL non-baseline implementations use `@DefaultBean` displacement
  (remove `@Alternative @Priority` from all of them and ensure only one non-`@DefaultBean` exists)
- Or keep the `@Alternative @Priority` chain intact and accept it as the mechanism
  for layer coexistence

Do not remove `@Alternative` from one bean without checking what other `@Alternative`
implementations exist for the same interface.

### Why this is non-obvious

Most developers reason about CDI alternatives in pairs: "my bean vs the default."
The three-way interaction (DefaultBean + Alternative(1) + Alternative(2)) is rarely
encountered, and the silent resolution change (no exception, wrong bean) gives no
diagnostic signal. The symptom (test assertion failure on unrelated data) is
completely disconnected from the cause (CDI annotation change).

### Why this fix

The obvious approach — "just remove the anti-pattern annotation" — is wrong because
it treats the annotations as decoration rather than as a load-bearing priority chain.
The fix requires understanding the full set of implementations and their annotation
interactions before changing any single one.

### Alternatives considered

- Remove `@Alternative @Priority(2)` from only the active bean → silently breaks resolution (this gotcha)
- Remove `@Alternative` from ALL implementations and use `@DefaultBean` displacement → requires ensuring exactly one non-`@DefaultBean` impl, and retiring or `@DefaultBean`-ing the intermediate layers
- Keep `@Alternative @Priority` chain as-is → accepted as the working mechanism until a coordinated cleanup addresses all implementations together

**See also:** GE-20260626-c21b02 — @DefaultBean suppression by any Instance<T> peer, a different silent failure in the same CDI displacement space.

entries.title: @DefaultBean + plain @ApplicationScoped enables CDI layer displacement without config switches or @Alternative @Priority
@Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException
entries.body:
@Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException

## @Alternative @Priority(n) in CDI 4.0/Quarkus globally activates the alternative — causes AmbiguousResolutionException

### Stack
Quarkus 3.31.1, CDI 4.0

### Symptom
Multiple beans implement the same SPI interface. Each alternative is annotated with
`@Alternative @Priority(10)` as well as `@ApplicationScoped`. On Quarkus startup, the
application fails with `AmbiguousResolutionException` — all implementations are active
simultaneously.

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ContextDiffStrategy
and qualifiers [@Default]: [TopLevelContextDiffStrategy, JsonPatchContextDiffStrategy, 
NoOpContextDiffStrategy]
```

### Context
SPI pattern where one default bean and two `@Alternative` beans implement an interface.
The intent was to activate one alternative at a time via
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `application.properties`.

### What was tried
Adding `@Priority(10)` alongside `@Alternative` — expected this to be a ranking hint
that would help CDI resolve ambiguity. Instead, `@Priority` on an `@Alternative` is what
globally activates the bean in CDI 4.0, making all three implementations simultaneously
active and causing the ambiguous resolution error.

### Root cause
In CDI 4.0 (Jakarta EE 10), `@Alternative @Priority(n)` is a shorthand for globally
activating an alternative across the entire application — no `beans.xml` or
`selected-alternatives` config needed. When ALL alternatives carry this annotation,
they are ALL active, which breaks injection points expecting a single bean.

### Solution 1 — Remove @Priority, use selected-alternatives config
**Approach:** Strip `@Priority` from all alternatives; activate one via config.
**Pros:** Per-profile/per-module control without code changes; the intended Quarkus mechanism for SPI switching.
**Cons:** Requires a config entry per activation; all alternatives default to inactive.

Remove `@Priority` from all `@Alternative` beans. Activate a specific alternative only
via `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` in `application.properties`:

```java
// WRONG — @Priority globally activates the alternative in CDI 4.0
@Alternative
@Priority(10)
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyAlternativeImpl implements MyInterface { ... }

// CORRECT — @Alternative only; activation controlled by config
@Alternative
@ApplicationScoped
public class MyAlternativeImpl implements MyInterface { ... }
```

```properties
# application.properties — activate the desired alternative
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.MyAlternativeImpl
```

### Solution 2 — Use different @Priority values to establish precedence
**Approach:** Keep `@Alternative @Priority` but assign distinct priority values; CDI resolves to the highest.
**Pros:** No config entry needed; the default (lowest priority) is always active, the override (highest priority) wins when present on the classpath. Works naturally for optional-module patterns where a higher-capability implementation should auto-replace the baseline.
**Cons:** All alternatives are always globally active (the core CDI 4.0 behaviour). The "default" must have the lowest priority; adding a third implementation requires careful priority assignment.

```java
// Default — always active; lowest priority loses when a higher one is present
@Alternative
@Priority(0)
@ApplicationScoped
public class ClaimFirstStrategy implements WorkerSelectionStrategy { ... }

// Override — higher priority wins; active only when on the classpath
@Alternative
@Priority(1)
@ApplicationScoped
public class SemanticWorkerSelectionStrategy implements WorkerSelectionStrategy { ... }
```

CDI injects the `@Priority(1)` bean when both are present; falls back to `@Priority(0)` when only
the default module is on the classpath. No `beans.xml` or `selected-alternatives` required.

**When to choose Solution 2 over Solution 1:** When the override is an optional module (not always
on the classpath) and the default must always be present. Config-based activation (Solution 1)
requires an explicit entry even for the default case; priority-based resolution (Solution 2) makes
the default zero-configuration.

### Why this is non-obvious
The `@Priority` annotation is commonly used alongside `@Alternative` in CDI tutorials
and examples from the CDI 2.x era, where `@Priority` on an alternative was a *ranking*
hint. In CDI 4.0 the semantics changed — `@Priority` on an `@Alternative` is now an
*activation* mechanism (equivalent to listing it in `beans.xml` with a priority). The
Quarkus docs for `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` don't warn about this interaction.

### Why this fix
`quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` gives per-profile/per-module control via config,
which is the intended Quarkus mechanism for SPI switching (same as how `PanningStrategyLoopControl`
and other engine SPIs are activated). It doesn't require code changes to switch backends.

**See also:** GE-20260422-ebb91d — AmbiguousResolutionException from multiple unqualified @ApplicationScoped beans

**See also:** GE-20260427-97650e "CDI ambiguity when adding second implementation of a quarkus-ledger repository interface"
**See also:** GE-20260427-62d3ab — use @Alternative @Priority(1) inner beans in @QuarkusTest to spy on SPI call sites
**See also:** [GE-20260427-c2b84f — @Alternative @Priority(1) beans in a test-helper jar are invisible to downstream @QuarkusTest — no Jandex index](GE-20260427-c2b84f.md)

### Update — Test-refactoring trap: two classes declaring the same @Alternative

During a test refactoring, if two `@QuarkusTest` classes *simultaneously* declare an
`@Alternative @Priority(2)` inner class implementing the same type, Quarkus boot fails
with `AmbiguousResolutionException` even though `mvn test-compile` passes cleanly. The
compile succeeds because both classes are syntactically valid; the CDI conflict only
surfaces at application startup.

entries.title: @DefaultBean silently suppressed by any Instance<T> peer — breaks multi-implementation SPI patterns
entries.body:
@DefaultBean silently suppressed by any Instance<T> peer — breaks multi-implementation SPI patterns

### Symptom
Agent drift checking silently stops working after adding `@DefaultBean` to `AgentDriftChecker` — no error, no warning. The bean is never injected.

### Context
`DeploymentActualStateAdapter` injects `Instance<NodeDriftChecker>` and builds a `Map<String, NodeDriftChecker>` keyed by `nodeType()`. Four implementations exist: `AgentDriftChecker`, `ChannelDriftChecker`, `CaseTypeDriftChecker`, `TrustPolicyDriftChecker`. Each serves a different `nodeType()` but all implement `NodeDriftChecker`.

The goal was to make `AgentDriftChecker` replaceable by a richer implementation via classpath presence — the standard `@DefaultBean` → `@Alternative @Priority(1)` pattern used successfully elsewhere (e.g. `NoOpAgentStateStore` → `InMemoryAgentStateStore`).

### Root cause
Quarkus `@DefaultBean` suppression operates on **bean types** (interface types), not concrete classes. When `AgentDriftChecker` is `@DefaultBean` and `ChannelDriftChecker` (also implementing `NodeDriftChecker`) is `@ApplicationScoped`, ArC sees a non-default bean with the same interface type and suppresses the `@DefaultBean` — regardless of the fact that they serve completely different runtime roles via `nodeType()`.

The `@DefaultBean` pattern is designed for **single-injection-point replacement**: one interface, one default, one override. It is incompatible with `Instance<T>` multi-bean collection where implementations are distinguished by a runtime discriminator.

### What was tried (didn't work)
1. `@DefaultBean` on `AgentDriftChecker` — suppressed by `ChannelDriftChecker` existing
2. `@Alternative @Priority(1)` on the replacement — both beans appear in `Instance<T>` iteration, `HashMap.put()` non-deterministic winner for the same `nodeType()` key

### Fix
Do not use `@DefaultBean` or `@Alternative` for multi-implementation SPI patterns collected via `Instance<T>`. Instead, either:
- Enrich the existing bean directly (no displacement needed)
- Add priority-aware resolution in the adapter: `checkers.merge(nodeType, checker, (existing, incoming) -> getPriority(incoming) > getPriority(existing) ? incoming : existing)`

### Why this is non-obvious
The `@DefaultBean` pattern works flawlessly for single-injection patterns throughout the codebase (6+ SPIs use it). The mental model — "default vanishes when a better one arrives" — is correct for that context. The failure mode here is that *any* `NodeDriftChecker` implementation (not just an agent-specific one) triggers suppression. No error, no warning, no log. The bean simply disappears from the `Instance<T>` iteration.

### Why this fix
Enriching the existing bean avoids all CDI displacement complexity. The comparison logic (pure Java utility) lives in the type-owning module; the SPI implementation stays in the consumer module unchanged. No CDI annotations change, no new beans, no Instance<T> interaction to reason about.

### Alternatives considered
- Priority-aware adapter resolution — works but adds complexity to the adapter for a problem that only exists because of the displacement pattern
- Bridge module with `@Alternative @Priority(1)` — both beans appear in Instance iteration; HashMap collision is non-deterministic
- Composition approach (AgentNodeSpec wrapping AgentDescriptor) — blocked by tenancyId being required in AgentDescriptor's compact constructor

**See also:** GE-20260623-c651a1 — removing @Alternative from one bean in a multi-implementation chain silently changes resolution, another CDI displacement gotcha.

entries.title: @DefaultBean @Unremovable required when injection point lives in a different Maven module
entries.body:
@DefaultBean @Unremovable required when injection point lives in a different Maven module

### Symptom

`jakarta.enterprise.inject.UnsatisfiedResolutionException` at augmentation time when using a Quarkus library module that defines a `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` SPI implementation. The exception says no bean is available for the injection type — but the bean class is clearly on the classpath and CDI-annotated.

No warning is emitted that the bean was eliminated. The error looks identical to a missing implementation.

### Context

A library is split across two Maven modules:

- `core` defines a SPI interface (`Foo`) and a `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped NoOpFoo implements Foo` default
- `mcp` depends on `core` and contains the only `@Inject Foo` injection point in the consuming app

An application adds both `core` and `mcp` as dependencies. Augmentation fails.

Concrete case: `casehub-connectors-core` defines `ConnectorMeshBridge` SPI and `NoOpConnectorMeshBridge @DefaultBean`. The injection point `@Inject ConnectorMeshBridge` lives only in `casehub-connectors-mcp` tool classes. Without `@Unremovable`, augmentation of an app using both modules throws `UnsatisfiedResolutionException`.

### Root cause

Quarkus ARC performs unused-bean elimination at build time. It scans for injection points within the module being augmented, but `@DefaultBean` implementations that have no injection point visible within the defining module itself are treated as unused and eliminated. ARC does not traverse sibling modules to discover injection points — it only sees what is compiled together in the augmentation classpath at that moment.

The result: the `@DefaultBean` bean is removed before the consuming app can inject it.

### Fix

Add `@Unremovable` to the `@DefaultBean` class:

```java
@DefaultBean
@Unremovable   // ← required: injection point is in a different Maven module (mcp)
@ApplicationScoped
public class NoOpConnectorMeshBridge implements ConnectorMeshBridge {
    @Override
    public void notifyDelivered(String connectorId, String destination, String content) {}
}
```

`@Unremovable` instructs ARC to retain the bean in the CDI graph regardless of whether a visible injection point is found.

### Why this is non-obvious

The `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` error message is identical whether the bean is absent from the classpath or has been eliminated by ARC. Nothing in the error output mentions bean removal. Developers familiar with `@Unremovable` associate it with extension-published beans (where the Quarkus docs describe it explicitly) — not with plain `@DefaultBean` library beans whose injection point happens to be in a sibling module.

The protocol `quarkus-extension-unremovable-consumer-beans.md` covers the extension case; this gotcha surfaces the same issue in non-extension library modules where the split is a Maven module boundary rather than an extension deployment boundary.

**See also:** [GE-20260531-9118e7](GE-20260531-9118e7.md) — runtime Maven scope on shared mock library silently expands CDI scan, breaking @DefaultBean suppression | [GE-20260515-ffde26](GE-20260515-ffde26.md) — optional Quarkus features: Jandex library module pattern | [GE-20260422-e48245](GE-20260422-e48245.md) — @DefaultBean lives in io.quarkus.arc | [GE-20260603-268164](GE-20260603-268164.md) — quarkus:build on library JAR forces CDI validation on compile-scope only
