@IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs
entries.body:
@IfBuildProfile + @Alternative + @Priority resolves CDI without selected-alternatives in indexed JARs

### Symptom

Adding a dev-profile-only CDI bean (e.g., a `CurrentPrincipal` for dev mode) via `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` causes startup failures — all beans from the non-profiled `quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives` list disappear.

### Context

Quarkus profile-specific properties (`%dev.`, `%test.`, `%prod.`) completely **replace** their non-profiled counterparts. If the base `application.properties` has:

```properties
quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=\
  com.example.JpaRepo,\
  com.example.JpaPlanItemStore,\
  com.example.JpaSubCaseGroupRepo
```

Adding `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=com.example.DevBean` drops all three JPA alternatives in dev mode — CDI startup fails with unsatisfied dependency errors for every bean that was in the original list.

### Root cause

Profile-specific properties in Quarkus are full replacements, not merges. This is by design (SmallRye Config behaviour), but the failure mode is silent — no warning that the non-profiled value was dropped.

### Fix

Use bean-level annotations instead of `selected-alternatives`:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@Alternative
@Priority(150)  // beats OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)
@IfBuildProfile("dev")
public class DemoCurrentPrincipal implements CurrentPrincipal {
    @Override public String tenancyId() { return "demo-tenant"; }
    @Override public String actorId()   { return "demo-user"; }
}
```

**Requirements:**
1. The bean must live in a **Jandex-indexed JAR** (e.g., the application's own `runtime/` module). ArC discovers it automatically — no `selected-alternatives` entry needed.
2. `@IfBuildProfile("dev")` excludes the bean entirely from non-dev builds — no ambiguity in production.
3. `@Priority(150)` resolves over competing `@Alternative` beans (e.g., `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Priority(100)`) via standard ArC priority resolution.

This is the same mechanism by which `OidcCurrentPrincipal @Alternative @Priority(100)` beats `MockCurrentPrincipal @DefaultBean` in production — without being listed in `selected-alternatives`.

### Why this is non-obvious

The natural instinct is `%dev.quarkus.arc.selected-alternatives=MyDevBean` — it looks like the standard profile-override pattern. The replacement behaviour is documented for SmallRye Config but not prominently flagged in the Quarkus CDI guide. The failure (dropped JPA alternatives) manifests as unrelated `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` errors that don't mention `selected-alternatives` at all.

### Why this fix

`@IfBuildProfile + @Priority` solves the problem at the bean level — no configuration property needed. The alternative (duplicating the full `selected-alternatives` list in every profile override) is fragile and drifts as new alternatives are added.

### Alternatives considered

- **Duplicate the full list in `%dev.`** — works but fragile; every new `@Alternative` bean must be added to every profile-specific override. Drifts silently.
- **Use `@UnlessBuildProfile("prod")` instead of `@IfBuildProfile("dev")`** — activates in both dev and test profiles, which may not be desired. Test profile has its own `FixedCurrentPrincipal @Priority(200)`.

entries.title: @DefaultBean in a module without quarkus-arc dependency is silently ignored — no-op bean never suppressed
entries.body:
@DefaultBean in a module without quarkus-arc dependency is silently ignored — no-op bean never suppressed

## Symptom

A `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped` no-op implementation is placed in an `api` module alongside its SPI interface. A consumer provides a real `@ApplicationScoped` implementation. When injected via `Instance<SpiInterface>`, CDI iterates both beans — the `@DefaultBean` is NOT suppressed by the consumer bean. The no-op runs alongside the real implementation.

No CDI ambiguity error at startup. No warning. The `@DefaultBean` annotation is simply not processed.

## Context

`@DefaultBean` is from `io.quarkus.arc.DefaultBean` — a Quarkus ARC extension annotation. For ARC to process it, the `quarkus-arc` dependency must be on the module's compile classpath. Pure-Java API modules typically do not declare `quarkus-arc` — they declare only `jakarta.enterprise.cdi-api` for `@ApplicationScoped`.

The class IS discovered by ARC (the module has a Jandex index), so the `@ApplicationScoped` annotation works. But the `@DefaultBean` annotation is not processed — ARC treats it as a regular bean.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` is processed by ARC's build-time augmentation. The augmentation reads the annotation from the Jandex index. If the annotation class (`io.quarkus.arc.DefaultBean`) is not in the Jandex index of the declaring module's dependencies, ARC cannot resolve it and silently ignores it.

## Fix

Place `@DefaultBean` no-op implementations in a module that has `quarkus-arc` as a compile dependency — typically `runtime/`. All other engine no-ops follow this pattern (`NoOpWorkerStatusListener`, `NoOpCaseChannelProvider`, etc. are in `runtime/internal/worker/`).

```
# Wrong — api/ has no quarkus-arc:
api/src/main/java/io/casehub/api/spi/NoOpFoo.java

# Right — runtime/ has quarkus-arc:
runtime/src/main/java/io/casehub/engine/internal/worker/NoOpFoo.java
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The class compiles, is discovered by CDI, and works as a bean. The only thing that doesn't work is the `@DefaultBean` semantics — and there is no error, warning, or log message indicating the annotation was ignored. The failure mode is that the no-op runs when it shouldn't, which in most cases is invisible (a no-op doing nothing alongside a real implementation is harmless — until it's iterated via `Instance<>`).

**See also:** [GE-20260523-afab1d](GE-20260523-afab1d.md) — @ApplicationScoped bean in JAR invisible to ARC without Jandex | [GE-20260515-fd3156](GE-20260515-fd3156.md) — @DefaultBean must be on @Produces method | [GE-20260427-543663](../quarkus/GE-20260427-543663.md) — @Produces @DefaultBean for library-level overridable defaults | [GE-20260604-81a6a6](GE-20260604-81a6a6.md) — @DefaultBean @Unremovable required cross-module | [GE-20260601-848232](GE-20260601-848232.md) — quarkus.arc.exclude-types silently does nothing for Jandex JARs

langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types
entries.body:
langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types

### What it is
`DeclarativeUtil` in `langchain4j-agentic` exposes a single static list `chatSupplierParameterResolvers` with one registration method `addChatSupplierParameterResolver(ChatSupplierParameterResolver)`. This resolver hook fires only during `@ChatModelSupplier` and `@StreamingChatModelSupplier` processing. All other supplier annotations (`@ToolsSupplier`, `@ChatMemorySupplier`, `@ChatMemoryProviderSupplier`, `@ContentRetrieverSupplier`, `@RetrievalAugmentorSupplier`, `@AgentListenerSupplier`, `@ToolProviderSupplier`) call `checkArguments(method)` which enforces **zero parameters** before invoking the static method directly — no resolver hook exists for these paths.

### Why this matters for framework integrators
Any DI framework (Quarkus, Spring, Guice) wanting to inject CDI/Spring beans into supplier methods is blocked for all supplier types except chat model suppliers. The `@CdiBean` workaround in `quarkus-langchain4j` only works for `@ChatModelSupplier` as a result. Users who need a CDI-managed `ContentRetriever` or `ChatMemory` must use `Arc.container()` or `ApplicationContext.getBean()` inside the static method body — bypassing injection, scope management, and testability.

### How to discover this
Only by decompiling `langchain4j-agentic-1.15.1-beta25.jar` and reading `DeclarativeUtil.class`. The library has no published Javadoc for internal classes and no documentation of the SPI surface area.

```bash
# Locate the JAR
find ~/.m2/repository/dev/langchain4j/langchain4j-agentic -name "*.jar" | grep -v sources | head -1

# The class structure reveals: addChatSupplierParameterResolver() is the only hook
# All other configureAgent() branches call checkArguments() then invokeStatic()
```

### Workaround
For Quarkus: use `SyntheticCreationalContext.getInjectedReference()` in the synthetic bean creator (`AgenticRecorder`) to inject CDI beans at agent construction time, bypassing the static supplier method entirely. This requires detecting at build time that no static supplier method exists for a given type, then adding a CDI injection point for that type.

### Upstream path
An upstream PR to `langchain4j-agentic` should propose a general `SupplierParameterResolver` SPI (not chat-model-specific) and add resolver hooks to all supplier type branches in `configureAgent()`. Frame as a DI-framework-agnostic improvement — Spring users would benefit from the same hook.

### Why this is non-obvious
The library name suggests platform independence (`langchain4j` not `langchain4j-spring`), so the assumption is that all supplier types are equally extensible. The asymmetry between `@ChatModelSupplier` (has a resolver hook) and all other supplier annotations (do not) is not mentioned in any README, Javadoc, or issue tracker. The class is package-private in the library with no stable API guarantee.

entries.title: Quarkus Arc @Alternative does not suppress injection point validation of displaced beans
entries.body:
Quarkus Arc @Alternative does not suppress injection point validation of displaced beans

### Symptom
Consumer `@QuarkusTest` fails with `UnsatisfiedResolutionException` for a dependency
(`ChatModel`) that only the production bean needs — even though an `@Alternative @Priority(1)`
test stub exists for the same SPI and would be selected.

### Context
`LlmQueryExpander` is `@ApplicationScoped` with `@IfBuildProperty(enableIfMissing=true)` — registered by default.
Its constructor requires `ChatModel`. `InMemoryQueryExpander` is `@Alternative @Priority(1)` implementing
the same `QueryExpander` SPI. In a `@QuarkusTest` without a `ChatModel` bean, the expectation is that
`InMemoryQueryExpander` replaces `LlmQueryExpander` and no `ChatModel` is needed.

### What was tried (didn't work)
Adding `InMemoryQueryExpander` as `@Alternative @Priority(1)` to the test classpath. The alternative
is correctly selected for `QueryExpander` injection points, but `LlmQueryExpander` is still a
registered bean and its `ChatModel` constructor parameter is still validated.

### Root cause
Quarkus Arc validates injection points of ALL registered beans at build time — not just the
selected bean for a given type. `@Alternative` controls which bean is injected at consumer
injection points, but does NOT suppress validation of other registered beans' own injection
points. A registered bean with an unsatisfied dependency causes a build failure regardless
of whether it would ever be instantiated.

### Fix
Two complementary approaches:

1. **Remove `enableIfMissing = true`** from `@IfBuildProperty` — require explicit mode
   selection so the heavy bean is only registered when the consumer explicitly opts in.

2. **Add a `@DefaultBean` no-op** that implements the SPI with zero dependencies.
   `@DefaultBean` is displaced by any `@ApplicationScoped` bean (when mode is set)
   or `@Alternative` (in tests). The no-op ensures a bean always exists without
   dragging in heavy transitive dependencies.

### Why this is non-obvious
The mental model of `@Alternative` suggests it "replaces" the original bean. In standard
CDI (Weld), this is closer to true — alternatives affect typesafe resolution. But Quarkus
Arc performs aggressive build-time validation of ALL registered beans' injection points,
including beans that will never be instantiated because a higher-priority alternative exists.
The distinction between "not selected" and "not registered" is invisible until it breaks.

entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j Ollama extension registers @Default ChatModel — clashes with @DefaultBean fallback

## Symptom

When the quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension is on the classpath alongside a
`@DefaultBean ChatModel` implementation, Quarkus throws at startup:

```
AmbiguousResolutionException: Ambiguous dependencies for type ChatModel and qualifiers [@Default]
  - CLASS bean [... AgentProviderChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
  - SYNTHETIC bean [... OllamaChatModel] qualifiers=[@Any, @Default]
```

## Context

A custom `@DefaultBean @ApplicationScoped ChatModel` implementation exists to serve as a
fallback (e.g. a Claude CLI bridge). The expectation is that adding the Ollama extension
places its `ChatModel` higher-priority, which should silence the `@DefaultBean`. Instead,
both are registered with `@Default` and Quarkus cannot choose between them.

## Root cause

`@DefaultBean` in Quarkus ARC means: "this bean is only active if no other `@Default`-
qualified bean of the same type is present." The mechanism works when the competing bean
is `@ApplicationScoped` with no explicit qualifier (which implicitly gets `@Default`), or
when the competing bean is annotated with `@Alternative @Priority(N)`. However, the
quarkus-langchain4j-ollama extension registers its model as a **SYNTHETIC bean with an
explicit `@Default` qualifier** — not as a higher-priority alternative. ARC sees two
explicit `@Default` beans and cannot resolve.

## Fix

Veto the `@DefaultBean` explicitly when the Ollama extension is active by pairing
`@IfBuildProperty` with `-Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false` at build time:

```java
@DefaultBean
@ApplicationScoped
@IfBuildProperty(name = "casehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled",
                 stringValue = "true", enableIfMissing = true)
class AgentProviderChatModel implements ChatModel { ... }
```

```bash
# Run with Ollama — veto the DefaultBean
mvn clean test -Peval,eval-ollama \
  -Dcasehub.eval.claude-provider.enabled=false \
  ...
```

`mvn clean` is required to force fresh augmentation when toggling this property (see
related entry on augmentation caching).

## Why this is non-obvious

`@DefaultBean` is marketed as "the bean that loses to any other bean of the same type."
In practice it only loses to beans that don't also carry an explicit `@Default` qualifier.
Quarkus LangChain4j provider extensions register SYNTHETIC beans with explicit `@Default`
rather than `@Alternative @Priority`, making the clash non-obvious. The `@DefaultBean`
javadoc does not describe this failure mode.

**See also:** [GE-20260601-fcf0d9](GE-20260601-fcf0d9.md) — two @DefaultBean beans for the same type → AmbiguousResolutionException | [GE-20260531-1ec900](GE-20260531-1ec900.md) — Quarkus ARC registers non-CDI abstract class as @Dependent bean

entries.body:
langchain4j-agentic DeclarativeUtil has a single CDI resolver hook for @ChatModelSupplier only — no equivalent for other supplier types

### What it is
`DeclarativeUtil` in `langchain4j-agentic` exposes a single static list `chatSupplierParameterResolvers` with one registration method `addChatSupplierParameterResolver(ChatSupplierParameterResolver)`. This resolver hook fires only during `@ChatModelSupplier` and `@StreamingChatModelSupplier` processing. All other supplier annotations (`@ToolsSupplier`, `@ChatMemorySupplier`, `@ChatMemoryProviderSupplier`, `@ContentRetrieverSupplier`, `@RetrievalAugmentorSupplier`, `@AgentListenerSupplier`, `@ToolProviderSupplier`) call `checkArguments(method)` which enforces **zero parameters** before invoking the static method directly — no resolver hook exists for these paths.

### Why this matters for framework integrators
Any DI framework (Quarkus, Spring, Guice) wanting to inject CDI/Spring beans into supplier methods is blocked for all supplier types except chat model suppliers. The `@CdiBean` workaround in `quarkus-langchain4j` only works for `@ChatModelSupplier` as a result. Users who need a CDI-managed `ContentRetriever` or `ChatMemory` must use `Arc.container()` or `ApplicationContext.getBean()` inside the static method body — bypassing injection, scope management, and testability.

### How to discover this
Only by decompiling `langchain4j-agentic-1.15.1-beta25.jar` and reading `DeclarativeUtil.class`. The library has no published Javadoc for internal classes and no documentation of the SPI surface area.

```bash
# Locate the JAR
find ~/.m2/repository/dev/langchain4j/langchain4j-agentic -name "*.jar" | grep -v sources | head -1

# The class structure reveals: addChatSupplierParameterResolver() is the only hook
# All other configureAgent() branches call checkArguments() then invokeStatic()
```

### Workaround
For Quarkus: use `SyntheticCreationalContext.getInjectedReference()` in the synthetic bean creator (`AgenticRecorder`) to inject CDI beans at agent construction time, bypassing the static supplier method entirely. This requires detecting at build time that no static supplier method exists for a given type, then adding a CDI injection point for that type.

### Upstream path
An upstream PR to `langchain4j-agentic` should propose a general `SupplierParameterResolver` SPI (not chat-model-specific) and add resolver hooks to all supplier type branches in `configureAgent()`. Frame as a DI-framework-agnostic improvement — Spring users would benefit from the same hook.

### Why this is non-obvious
The library name suggests platform independence (`langchain4j` not `langchain4j-spring`), so the assumption is that all supplier types are equally extensible. The asymmetry between `@ChatModelSupplier` (has a resolver hook) and all other supplier annotations (do not) is not mentioned in any README, Javadoc, or issue tracker. The class is package-private in the library with no stable API guarantee.

LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation
entries.body:
LangChain4j Anthropic: ResponseFormat.JSON without schema throws UnsupportedFeatureException — not a degradation

## Symptom

Passing `ResponseFormat.JSON` (type only, no schema) to `ChatRequest.builder().responseFormat(...)` for an Anthropic-backed `ChatModel` throws `UnsupportedFeatureException` rather than silently degrading or prompting.

## Context

`InternalAnthropicHelper.validate(ChatRequestParameters)` is called inside `AnthropicChatModel.doChat()` before any API call is made. The validation checks:

```java
if (parameters.responseFormat() != null
        && parameters.responseFormat().type() == ResponseFormatType.JSON
        && parameters.responseFormat().jsonSchema() == null) {
    throw new UnsupportedFeatureException(...);
}
```

This means JSON mode without a schema is explicitly rejected at the LangChain4j layer — it never reaches the Anthropic API.

## Root cause

Anthropic's native API requires a JSON schema to enforce structured output. Unlike OpenAI (which supports a bare JSON mode that produces valid but unstructured JSON), Anthropic has no schema-less JSON mode. LangChain4j's Anthropic integration reflects this correctly by refusing the schemaless request rather than silently ignoring the constraint.

## Fix

Always pair `ResponseFormat.JSON` with a `JsonSchema` when using Anthropic:

```java
ResponseFormat responseFormat = ResponseFormat.builder()
    .type(ResponseFormatType.JSON)
    .jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
        .name("MySchema")
        .rootElement(JsonObjectSchema.builder()
            .addStringProperty("field", "Description")
            .required("field")
            .build())
        .build())
    .build();
```

For a broad catch on provider-specific failures (including older Claude models that don't support structured output at all), wrap the `llm.chat(request)` call in `catch (Exception e)` and degrade gracefully:

```java
try {
    ChatResponse response = llm.chat(request);
    return Optional.of(parse(response.aiMessage().text()));
} catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("Structured enrichment failed ({}), falling back to structural rendering", e.getMessage());
    return Optional.empty();
}
```

## Why this is non-obvious

The LangChain4j docs describe `ResponseFormat.JSON` as a valid type value. There is no public documentation on which providers support it with or without a schema. The `UnsupportedFeatureException` is thrown before any network call, so there is no HTTP error to debug — it looks like an in-process configuration error with no obvious connection to the Anthropic API's structured output requirements.

The `supportedCapabilities()` mechanism exists on `ChatModel` for high-level AI Services to check before using JSON schema, but `ClaudeMarkdownRenderer`-style code calling the low-level `ChatModel.chat(ChatRequest)` API bypasses that guard entirely.

### Why this fix

`ResponseFormat.JSON` with `JsonSchema` is the only valid combination for Anthropic. Adding a schema is not optional — it is the required API surface.

entries.title: @LookupIfProperty for conditional CDI bean activation via Instance<> — cleaner than inert-bean pattern
entries.body:
@LookupIfProperty for conditional CDI bean activation via Instance<> — cleaner than inert-bean pattern

### Context
A Quarkus application ships multiple provider implementations of an SPI (e.g. `DeviceProvider`) in one Docker image. Each provider should be independently enableable via config (`provider.enabled=true/false`). Disabled providers must be invisible to `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration — not just "present but returning empty results."

### What a skilled developer would normally do
Guard in `@PostConstruct`: check `enabled`, skip initialization if false. Make every method return a no-op result (`discover()` → empty list, `dispatch()` → FAILED, `status()` → DISCONNECTED). This is the "inert-bean" pattern — the bean exists but does nothing.

Problems with inert beans:
- The bean IS discovered by `Instance<DeviceProvider>` — callers see a broken provider
- `@PostConstruct` still runs (and may fail if config properties are missing)
- Every method needs guard logic
- SmallRye Config still validates all `@ConfigMapping` properties at startup (see GE-20260626-e0ecaf)

### Technique
Use `@LookupIfProperty` from Quarkus ARC:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@LookupIfProperty(name = "casehub.iot.homeassistant.enabled", stringValue = "true")
public class HomeAssistantProvider implements DeviceProvider { ... }
```

When `enabled` is absent or `false`:
- The bean is never instantiated
- `@PostConstruct` never runs
- `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration skips it entirely
- No guard logic needed in any method

Combined with `Optional<String>` on all `@ConfigMapping` properties (GE-20260626-e0ecaf), this allows disabled providers to exist on the classpath without causing config validation failures or appearing in the provider registry.

### Why this is non-obvious
`@LookupIfProperty` is less well-known than `@IfBuildProperty` (which is build-time only and prevents runtime reconfiguration). The naming — "lookup if" vs "if build" — doesn't clearly convey the difference. Many developers reach for `@IfBuildProperty` first, discover it prevents runtime toggling in Docker images, and then fall back to the inert-bean pattern instead of finding `@LookupIfProperty`.

Testing — Principles
entries.body:
A bug fixed without a test will recur.

---

## Coverage Analysis

**Line coverage is a floor, not a ceiling.** 80% line coverage with no
robustness tests is worse than 60% with comprehensive edge-case coverage.

After writing tests for a feature, explicitly ask:

> "What would have to go wrong in production that my tests would NOT catch?"

Every answer is a missing test.

Keep asking until the answer is "nothing credible."

### Coverage is inadequate when:

- All tests still pass after deleting the function body
- No test triggers any catch block or error handler
- No test asserts a specific return value (only that no exception was thrown)
- Mocks outnumber real I/O calls
- Every test is a unit test with no integration or E2E coverage

### Coverage analysis checklist

Run this after writing tests for any feature:

- [ ] Happy path verified with specific output assertion?
- [ ] Every error branch triggered by at least one test?
- [ ] Boundary values (empty, null, max, min) explicitly tested?
- [ ] Real I/O paths exercised (not only mocked)?
- [ ] Regression test exists if this is a bug fix?
- [ ] Mutation check: if I flip a `>` to `>=`, delete a return statement, or remove a condition — would a test catch it? If not, an assertion is missing.

---

## Test Flakiness Prevention

A flaky test — one that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without code
changes — is worse than no test. It erodes trust in the suite and causes real
failures to be ignored as "probably flaky."

**Apply this section when any of these are present:**

| Trigger | Risk |
|---------|------|
| Async / concurrent code | Race between assertion and completion |
| External services (HTTP, DB, queue) | Timing, network, or ordering variability |
| Date/time dependencies | Results differ by time of day or timezone |
| Shared mutable state between tests | Test-order dependency; passes in isolation, fails in suite |
| Random number generation | Non-deterministic output |
| File system with non-isolated paths | Leftover state from previous run |

**Rules:**
- Never use `sleep()` to wait for async completion — use explicit awaits, callbacks, or polling with a timeout
- Never share mutable state between tests — reset or isolate per test
- Never depend on test execution order — each test must be independent
- Seed or mock random number generators in tests that consume them
- Use injected/fixed clocks for date/time-sensitive logic, never `Date.now()` or `datetime.now()` directly
- Use isolated temp directories per test, never hardcoded paths

**If a test is already flaky:** fix the root cause (race condition, shared state) rather than adding retries. Retries hide the problem; they don't solve it.

---

## High-Value Test Prioritization

Not all tests have equal value. When time is limited:

| Priority | Test type | Reason |
|----------|-----------|--------|
| **1** | E2E for core user flows | High blast radius; catches integration failures invisible to lower layers |
| **2** | Integration tests for I/O paths | Catches wiring bugs; mocks cannot |
| **3** | Robustness / error path tests | Most production bugs are edge cases |
| **4** | Happy path unit tests | Fast feedback for logic-heavy code |
| **5** | Trivial delegation, getters/setters | Skip — near-zero bug-catching value |

Skip Priority 5 entirely. Testing trivial delegation adds maintenance burden
with no meaningful protection.

---

## UI Testing Mandate — Browser Automation Required

**A UI component or page is not tested until a browser has exercised it.**

Visual showcases, static HTML previews, and component demos are documentation,
not tests. They do not verify the feature works. Use Playwright (TypeScript
projects) or the appropriate browser automation tool for the stack.

### Required for any web UI change

At minimum, one browser test covering the happy path:

```typescript
test('user can submit the form', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/the-page');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Success')).toBeVisible();
});
```

### Browser tests must cover

| Scenario | What to assert |
|----------|----------------|
| Happy path | Primary action succeeds; correct UI state appears |
| Validation | Invalid input shows specific error message |
| Async/loading | Loading state visible, then resolved state appears |
| Error state | Server error shows user-facing message, not a crash or blank screen |

### What is NOT acceptable as a UI test

- "Component rendered without throwing" — no behavioral assertion
- A static HTML file opened manually — not a running server, not repeatable
- Screenshots without assertions — documents output, doesn't verify it
- Prose description of manual testing — not automated, not repeatable

If browser automation is not set up in the project, set it up before claiming
any UI work is complete.

---

## Common Pitfalls

| Mistake | Why It's Wrong | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| Mocking all dependencies | Tests verify mock behavior, not real behavior; wiring bugs invisible | Use real implementations for integration tests |
| Testing implementation, not behavior | Tests break on refactor even when behavior unchanged | Assert outcomes, not internal method calls |
| Only happy path tests | Edge cases cause most production bugs | Explicitly write robustness tests per the table above |
| Skipping browser tests for "simple" UI | Browser environment is unpredictable; "simple" still breaks | One Playwright happy path test is mandatory |
| High line coverage = done | Lines ≠ behaviors; error paths often not covered | Run the coverage analysis checklist above |
| Asserting no exception, not correct output | Tests pass even when function returns wrong value | Always assert the specific expected value |

---

## See Also

- `~/.hortora/garden/approaches/code-review.md` — Code review principles (testing section covers TDD enforcement at review time)

PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY @QuarkusTest: subscribe to unfiltered stream to confirm channel active before asserting on filtered results
entries.body:
PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY @QuarkusTest: subscribe to unfiltered stream to confirm channel active before asserting on filtered results

## Symptom

A `@QuarkusTest` integration test for a PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY broadcaster
fails intermittently with `ConditionTimeoutException` — the awaitility condition
times out even though the test logic is correct and passing in most CI runs. The
same commit SHA shows both pass and fail on successive runs.

## Context

`PostgresWorkItemEventBroadcaster.startListening()` is annotated `@PostConstruct`.
It issues a `LISTEN <channel>` command via the Vert.x reactive PG client — an async
call that returns immediately; the LISTEN is established on the Vert.x event loop
after control returns to the caller. Quarkus marks the application ready after all
`@PostConstruct` calls return, but does not wait for their async work to complete.

Tests that subscribe to a filtered stream and immediately fire events may do so
before the LISTEN is registered with PostgreSQL. Events published via `pg_notify`
reach the subscriber connection only after LISTEN is active — events fired before
that are silently dropped.

## What was tried (didn't work)

Increasing the awaitility timeout from 5 seconds to 10 seconds: reduced flake
frequency but did not eliminate it (the root cause is the LISTEN not being active,
not the notify→receive path being slow).

## Fix — Warm-up probe

Before subscribing to the filtered stream, subscribe to the **unfiltered** stream and
wait for a known event to arrive. This confirms the LISTEN channel is established and
the full async path (pg_notify → subscriber connection → BroadcastProcessor) is working:

```java
// 1. Subscribe to unfiltered stream BEFORE creating any items
final List<WorkItemLifecycleEvent> warmup = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
broadcaster.stream(null, null).subscribe().with(warmup::add);

// 2. Create the target item and wait for its CREATED event to arrive
final WorkItem target = createWorkItem("Target item");
Awaitility.await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
        .until(() -> warmup.stream().anyMatch(e -> target.id.equals(e.workItemId())));

// 3. LISTEN channel confirmed active — now subscribe to the filtered stream
final List<WorkItemLifecycleEvent> received = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
broadcaster.stream(target.id, null).subscribe().with(received::add);

// 4. Proceed with the test (noise items, claims, assertions)
```

The `BroadcastProcessor` is a hot stream — events emitted before subscription are
lost. Subscribing before creating any items ensures the warm-up probe captures the
CREATED event and the subsequent filtered subscription captures all later events.

## Why this is non-obvious

The application appears fully ready (HTTP is serving, CDI is wired) when the tests
start. The `@PostConstruct` has returned. There is no visible gap — but the LISTEN
command is in flight on the Vert.x event loop and may not have been acknowledged by
PostgreSQL yet. The failure only appears when the first `pg_notify` fires before that
acknowledgement arrives, which depends on container startup speed and event loop
scheduling in CI.

Bumping the awaitility timeout is the instinctive fix but addresses the wrong problem.
The test doesn't need more time to wait for the result — it needs to confirm the
infrastructure is ready before generating the result.

Quarkus extension testing module creates circular Maven dependency — InMemory stores unavailable in runtime unit tests
entries.body:
Quarkus extension testing module creates circular Maven dependency — InMemory stores unavailable in runtime unit tests

### Symptom

Attempting to use `InMemoryFooStore` from the extension's `testing` module in a unit test inside `runtime/src/test/` causes a Maven compile error: circular dependency detected.

### Context

Occurs in Quarkus extension projects structured as:
- `runtime/` — main runtime module with SPI interfaces
- `testing/` — utility module providing InMemory implementations of runtime SPIs for consumer unit tests

The testing module is designed for projects that *embed* the extension, not for the extension's own internal runtime tests.

### Root cause

The Maven dependency graph creates a cycle:
```
testing → runtime   (testing implements runtime SPIs — must depend on runtime)
runtime/src/test → testing   ← CYCLE
```

Maven detects this at compile time and rejects the build. The InMemory stores live in `testing` which already depends on `runtime`.

### Fix

For unit tests of runtime classes that need SPI implementations:

1. **Mockito** — mock the SPI directly and stub only the methods you need:
   ```java
   InstanceService svc = Mockito.mock(InstanceService.class);
   when(svc.findByInstanceId("worker-1")).thenReturn(Optional.of(instance));
   ```

2. **Inline stub** — create an anonymous class or static inner class inside the test:
   ```java
   InstanceStore store = new InstanceStore() {
       @Override public Optional<Instance> findByInstanceId(String id) {
           return id.equals("worker-1") ? Optional.of(instance) : Optional.empty();
       }
       // ...other methods
   };
   ```

Never import from the `testing` module in `runtime/src/test/`. The InMemory stores from `testing` are for consumer integration tests only.

### Why this is non-obvious

The testing module's InMemory stores look exactly like what you'd want for isolated unit tests — they're named `InMemory*Store`, they implement the right interfaces, and they're clearly intended for testing. Nothing in the naming or documentation signals that they can't be used from within the extension itself. The circular dependency only becomes apparent when Maven rejects the compile — there's no IDE warning before the build runs.

**See also:** [GE-20260424-318ef3](GE-20260424-318ef3.md) — service unit tests can't go in runtime/src/test/ when service depends on testing module | [GE-20260512-c30f52](GE-20260512-c30f52.md) — @QuarkusIntegrationTest in runtime module causes class loading failures

entries.title: quarkus-langchain4j-core Quarkus extension stalls @QuarkusTest augmentation when no model provider is configured
entries.body:
quarkus-langchain4j-core Quarkus extension stalls @QuarkusTest augmentation when no model provider is configured

## Symptom

`mvn test` hangs indefinitely during Quarkus augmentation when `quarkus-langchain4j-core` is a compile-scope dependency of a non-extension library module and no AI model provider is configured. No error message, no timeout — the build just blocks.

## Context

Occurs when a library module (Jandex-indexed, not a full Quarkus extension) adds `io.quarkiverse.langchain4j:quarkus-langchain4j-core` as a compile dependency to use the `EmbeddingModel` interface. During `@QuarkusTest` augmentation, the Quarkus extension activates and waits for a model provider that never arrives.

## What was tried

Adding `quarkus-langchain4j-core` as a `provided` scope — still stalls because the extension's deployment artifact is resolved transitively during augmentation.

## Root cause

`quarkus-langchain4j-core` is a Quarkus extension (has both runtime and deployment jars). When it appears on the augmentation classpath, Quarkus activates it and expects at least one model provider (OpenAI, Ollama, etc.) to be configured. Without one, augmentation stalls waiting for the CDI bean to resolve.

## Fix

Use `dev.langchain4j:langchain4j-core` (the plain Java library, **not** the Quarkus extension) as the compile dependency. This provides the `EmbeddingModel` interface for compilation without triggering Quarkus extension activation:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>dev.langchain4j</groupId>
  <artifactId>langchain4j-core</artifactId>
  <version>1.13.0</version>
</dependency>
```

For CDI injection, use `Instance<EmbeddingModel>` instead of `@Inject EmbeddingModel`:

```java
@Inject
public MyBean(final Instance<EmbeddingModel> modelInstance) {
    this.model = modelInstance.isResolvable() ? modelInstance.get() : null;
}
```

When no provider is configured, `instance.isResolvable()` returns `false` gracefully. The consuming app brings `quarkus-langchain4j-openai` (or any other provider extension), which satisfies the CDI bean at their own augmentation time.

## Why this is non-obvious

The symptom is a hang with no error — not a compilation failure or a clear exception. The natural instinct is to add the Quarkus extension for its CDI integration, but the correct separation is: library module uses the plain Java API, consuming application brings the Quarkus extension.

### Why this fix

The plain Java `langchain4j-core` provides the same `EmbeddingModel` interface without triggering extension activation. `Instance<EmbeddingModel>` makes the dependency optional at CDI resolution time, so the library works both with and without a configured provider.

**See also:** GE-20260422-3242bf — Use Instance<T> for optional CDI injection — resolves gracefully when no bean exists

### Alternatives considered

- `provided` scope: still triggers augmentation because the extension's deployment artifact is resolved transitively
- Mocking `EmbeddingModel` via `@InjectMock` in every `@QuarkusTest`: works but requires all existing tests to be updated

### Context
A Quarkus application ships multiple provider implementations of an SPI (e.g. `DeviceProvider`) in one Docker image. Each provider should be independently enableable via config (`provider.enabled=true/false`). Disabled providers must be invisible to `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration — not just "present but returning empty results."

### What a skilled developer would normally do
Guard in `@PostConstruct`: check `enabled`, skip initialization if false. Make every method return a no-op result (`discover()` → empty list, `dispatch()` → FAILED, `status()` → DISCONNECTED). This is the "inert-bean" pattern — the bean exists but does nothing.

Problems with inert beans:
- The bean IS discovered by `Instance<DeviceProvider>` — callers see a broken provider
- `@PostConstruct` still runs (and may fail if config properties are missing)
- Every method needs guard logic
- SmallRye Config still validates all `@ConfigMapping` properties at startup (see GE-20260626-e0ecaf)

### Technique
Use `@LookupIfProperty` from Quarkus ARC:

```java
@ApplicationScoped
@LookupIfProperty(name = "casehub.iot.homeassistant.enabled", stringValue = "true")
public class HomeAssistantProvider implements DeviceProvider { ... }
```

When `enabled` is absent or `false`:
- The bean is never instantiated
- `@PostConstruct` never runs
- `Instance<DeviceProvider>` iteration skips it entirely
- No guard logic needed in any method

Combined with `Optional<String>` on all `@ConfigMapping` properties (GE-20260626-e0ecaf), this allows disabled providers to exist on the classpath without causing config validation failures or appearing in the provider registry.

### Why this is non-obvious
`@LookupIfProperty` is less well-known than `@IfBuildProperty` (which is build-time only and prevents runtime reconfiguration). The naming — "lookup if" vs "if build" — doesn't clearly convey the difference. Many developers reach for `@IfBuildProperty` first, discover it prevents runtime toggling in Docker images, and then fall back to the inert-bean pattern instead of finding `@LookupIfProperty`.

entries.title: Quarkus Arc resolves CDI cycles between @ApplicationScoped beans via client proxies — even with constructor injection
entries.body:
Quarkus Arc resolves CDI cycles between @ApplicationScoped beans via client proxies — even with constructor injection

### Symptom
Code review flags a CDI cycle between two `@ApplicationScoped` beans as Critical — "application will not start." The cycle exists in the injection graph: `A → B (constructor injection) → A`. But the full build and all `@QuarkusTest` suites pass without any startup error.

### Context
`MessageService` (`@ApplicationScoped`) was given a field-injected `ChannelGateway`. `ChannelGateway` (`@ApplicationScoped`) already constructor-injected `MessageService` for its inbound dispatch paths (`receiveHumanMessage`, `receiveObserverSignal`). The cycle: `MessageService → ChannelGateway → MessageService`.

### What was tried
Code reviewer flagged the cycle as Critical, citing CDI startup failure. Using `Instance<ChannelGateway>` (lazy injection) to break it was considered as a fix.

### Root cause
The concern is correct for **pseudo-scoped** beans (`@Dependent`) which cannot be proxied — CDI cannot create a client proxy for a dependent-scoped bean, so a cycle involving one causes startup failure.

For **normal-scoped** beans (`@ApplicationScoped`, `@RequestScoped`, `@SessionScoped`), CDI mandates that the container MUST be able to create a client proxy. Quarkus Arc honors this: when `ChannelGateway`'s constructor is called, it receives a client proxy for `MessageService` — not the actual instance. The proxy is valid immediately; the actual `MessageService` instance is only resolved on the first method call. Both beans initialize without needing the other to exist first.

### Fix
Ensure all beans in the cycle are normal-scoped. Add a comment explaining the deliberate cycle so reviewers don't flag it:

```java
// Deliberate CDI cycle: MessageService → ChannelGateway → MessageService
// (via ChannelGateway.receiveHumanMessage / receiveObserverSignal).
// Both are @ApplicationScoped (normal scope). Arc resolves via client proxies —
// verified by full build and @QuarkusTest suite.
@Inject
ChannelGateway channelGateway;
```

### Why this is non-obvious
Most developers associate "CDI cycle" with startup failure. The distinction — pseudo-scoped vs normal-scoped — is in the spec but rarely surfaced in error messages or tutorials. The symptom that triggered the concern (a code reviewer calling it Critical) is exactly what skilled developers would say if they didn't know about proxy-based cycle resolution.

### Why this fix
A client proxy is the CDI-correct solution. Using `Instance<T>` (lazy injection) also works but adds indirection and a `.get()` call at every use site. Proxy resolution is transparent — callers don't change. Only use `Instance<T>` when a pseudo-scoped bean is in the cycle and proxy creation isn't possible.

**See also:** [GE-20260422-53d0f7](GE-20260422-53d0f7.md) — JPA @EntityListeners can be @ApplicationScoped CDI beans in Quarkus

**See also:** [GE-20260530-385dbb](GE-20260530-385dbb.md) — @Provider @ApplicationScoped on ClientRequestFilter bypasses CDI injection in Quarkus @RegisterRestClient

entries.body:
@All List<T> in Quarkus/ArC gives testable multi-bean injection without Instance<T>

## Context
When building a registry or routing layer that needs all CDI beans of a type
(e.g. routing to the right `Connector` by id), the natural CDI approach is
`Instance<T>`. But `Instance<T>` is a CDI interface with many abstract methods
— difficult to stub in plain JUnit tests without a full container.

## What developers normally do
Inject `Instance<T>`, iterate with `.stream()`, or use `@InjectMock` inside a
`@QuarkusTest` — both require a CDI container.

## The technique
Inject `@All List<T>` instead. ArC populates it at startup with all discovered
beans. In tests, pass `List.of(...)` directly to the constructor — no CDI
context, no mocking of `Instance<T>`, no `@QuarkusTest` needed.

```java
// Production: ArC populates this automatically
ConnectorService(@All List<Connector> connectors) {
    this.registry = connectors.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Connector::id, Function.identity()));
}

// Test: plain JUnit, no CDI
new ConnectorService(List.of(new SlackConnector(), new TeamsConnector()));
```

## Why this is non-obvious
`Instance<T>` is the CDI standard; `@All` is ArC-specific and not prominently
documented for this use case. The standard guidance says to use `@QuarkusTest`
for CDI testing. `@All List<T>` sidesteps the container requirement entirely
for patterns where the bean set is static at startup.

## Constraints
Requires `io.quarkus.arc.All`. Only works when the bean set is consumed at
construction time (static registry). Not suitable if beans are added/removed
at runtime.

**See also:** [GE-20260604-2f0889](GE-20260604-2f0889.md) — @Alternative @Priority(N) stubs appear in @All List<T> alongside original bean — not as replacements (gotcha when combining these patterns)

**See also:** [GE-20260529-ab148d](GE-20260529-ab148d.md) — multiple CDI constructors without @Inject → UnsatisfiedResolutionException (related CDI injection gotcha)

**See also:** [GE-20260609-75e00d](GE-20260609-75e00d.md) — package-private test constructor + @PostConstruct null guard technique

**See also:** [GE-20260614-efee3b](GE-20260614-efee3b.md) — SyntheticBeanBuildItem without addInjectionPoint compiles but fails at runtime

entries.title: CDI this.method() call bypasses @Transactional proxy — annotation silently dead on delegating overloads
entries.body:
CDI this.method() call bypasses @Transactional proxy — annotation silently dead on delegating overloads

## CDI this.method() call bypasses @Transactional proxy — annotation silently dead on delegating overloads

**ID:** GE-20260513-a49d06
**Stack:** Quarkus 3.x, ArC CDI, Java 21
**Symptom:** `@Transactional` on the inner of two delegating overloads has no effect. No error. Runtime behaviour is correct (the outer transaction covers everything), but the inner annotation is dead code that misleads future direct callers.
**Context:** A delegating overload pattern — a 4-arg method calls `this.instantiate(5-arg, null)` to supply a default. Both methods are annotated `@Transactional`. The 5-arg's annotation silently does nothing when reached via the delegation.

### What was tried (didn't work)
- Annotating both overloads with `@Transactional` — looks correct, annotation on the inner method is ignored
- Trusting that `@Transactional` on a method in an `@ApplicationScoped` bean always fires — it does, but only via the CDI proxy (external calls)

### Root cause
Quarkus ArC generates a CDI proxy subclass that wraps methods with interceptor chains. `@Transactional` is one such interceptor. Interceptors only fire when the call enters through the proxy — i.e., an external caller invokes the method on the injected bean reference.

When you call `this.method()` from within the bean, you bypass the proxy entirely and call the real instance directly. The interceptor chain for the inner method never executes. The outer method's transaction is already active and covers the inner call correctly — so runtime behaviour is correct — but the annotation on the inner method is dead code.

### Fix
Annotate only the outermost entry point. Remove `@Transactional` from the inner delegated method, or add a comment:

```java
@Transactional  // active only when called directly via CDI proxy
public WorkItem instantiate(WorkItemTemplate template, String titleOverride,
        String assigneeIdOverride, String createdBy, String callerRef) { ... }
```

If the inner method genuinely needs its own transaction boundary for direct external callers, use self-injection to force proxy routing:

```java
@Inject
MyService self;  // injects the CDI proxy, not `this`

public WorkItem outerMethod(...) {
    return self.innerMethod(...);  // interceptors fire
}
```

### Why this fix
Self-injection is the only way to force proxy interception on an intra-bean call. Most developers annotate both methods and assume both annotations fire — removing the redundant annotation from the inner method and adding a comment is the minimal correct fix that eliminates the false guarantee.

### Alternatives considered
- Annotate only the 5-arg (inner) and remove from 4-arg — wrong: the outer annotation is the one that actually fires
- Use `@Inject MyService self` self-injection — correct, but adds a circular dependency warning and complexity; only needed if the inner method must have its own independent transaction boundary

### Why this is non-obvious
Both methods appear correctly annotated. The runtime behaviour IS correct — no data corruption, no missing transaction. The failure mode is future: a developer who reads the code, sees `@Transactional` on the inner method, and calls it directly without a surrounding transaction gets no protection they were led to expect. The annotation creates a false contract that the CDI proxy never enforces.

*Score: 12/15 · Included because: consistently misleads developers, applies to all Quarkus CDI beans with delegating overloads, no error surfaced at runtime · Reservation: none*

**See also:** [GE-20260518-069f64](GE-20260518-069f64.md) — calling @Transactional method via this inside Mutiny lambda — use CDI self-injection

**See also:** [GE-20260604-d08c9f](GE-20260604-d08c9f.md) — @Transactional and @Tool can coexist on same method (technique)

**See also:** [GE-20260607-1ebb9c](GE-20260607-1ebb9c.md) — @Transactional on @PostConstruct is silently ignored — Arc proxy not created yet

entries.title: casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409
entries.body:
casehub-work IllegalStateExceptionMapper silently maps IllegalStateException to HTTP 409

### Symptom

REST endpoint returns HTTP 409 Conflict instead of the expected 500 Internal Server Error.
Happens when application code throws `IllegalStateException` for an infrastructure failure
(poll timeout, misconfiguration, unresolvable dependency).

### Context

Any application that depends on `casehub-work` and throws `IllegalStateException` from a
REST-invoked code path.

### Root cause

`casehub-work` JAR ships `io.casehub.work.runtime.api.IllegalStateExceptionMapper` — a
`jakarta.ws.rs.ext.ExceptionMapper<IllegalStateException>` that maps every
`IllegalStateException` to HTTP 409 Conflict. The mapper is registered globally via CDI
and affects any `IllegalStateException` thrown during a REST request in the application,
not just ones thrown from casehub-work code itself.

### Fix

Use a different exception type for infrastructure failures that should produce 500:

```java
// ❌ Produces HTTP 409 — mapped by casehub-work's IllegalStateExceptionMapper
throw new IllegalStateException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);

// ✅ Produces HTTP 500 — no mapper for generic RuntimeException
throw new RuntimeException("Agent did not reply for correlationId=" + id);
```

Alternatively, register a `@Priority(1)` exception mapper that overrides casehub-work's
for specific exception subtypes, or use a custom exception class that extends
`RuntimeException` directly.

### Why this is non-obvious

The mapper is shipped inside a transitive JAR (`casehub-work-0.2-SNAPSHOT.jar`) and is
nowhere documented. The symptom (409 instead of 500) gives no hint that an exception
mapper is involved — 409 Conflict is semantically about resource state, so developers
naturally investigate their domain logic rather than exception infrastructure. The 5-second
delay before the 409 (from a poll timeout) makes the connection even harder to spot.

jackson-databind alone causes @QuarkusTest class-loading failure in downstream modules — quarkus-jackson provides the CDI ObjectMapper producer
entries.body:
jackson-databind alone causes @QuarkusTest class-loading failure in downstream modules — quarkus-jackson provides the CDI ObjectMapper producer

A Quarkus library module adds `jackson-databind` as a compile dependency and
creates a `@ApplicationScoped` CDI bean that injects `ObjectMapper` via `@Inject`.
The library's own unit tests pass (plain JUnit, no CDI container). The full
reactor build fails with a class-loading error in a **downstream** module that
runs `@QuarkusTest`.

### Symptom

```
TestEngine with ID 'junit-jupiter' encountered a critical issue during test discovery:
ClassSelector [className = '...WebhookRouterTest'] resolution failed
Cause: PreconditionViolationException: Could not load class with name: ...WebhookRouterTest
```

The error is a class-loading failure in a module that **did not change**. No
"UnsatisfiedResolutionException" or "missing producer" message appears. The
failure looks like a test infrastructure problem, not a dependency issue.

### Root cause

Quarkus augmentation in the downstream module discovers the library's CDI bean
via Jandex (the library has the `jandex-maven-plugin`). ArC tries to resolve
the `ObjectMapper` injection point. `jackson-databind` provides the
`ObjectMapper` class but **no CDI producer**. The producer comes from
`quarkus-jackson` (or `quarkus-rest-jackson`). Without either on the classpath,
augmentation fails during class resolution — surfacing as a class-loading error,
not a CDI error.

### Fix

Replace `jackson-databind` with `quarkus-jackson` in the library module's
`pom.xml`. `quarkus-jackson` transitively includes `jackson-databind` and
provides the `ObjectMapper` CDI producer. It does NOT pull in REST
infrastructure (unlike `quarkus-rest-jackson`).

```xml
<!-- ❌ BAD: compiles but breaks downstream @QuarkusTest -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.fasterxml.jackson.core</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- ✅ GOOD: provides ObjectMapper CDI producer -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
    <artifactId>quarkus-jackson</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

### Why this is non-obvious

Three layers of indirection hide the root cause:

1. The library's own tests pass — they create `ObjectMapper` manually, no CDI
2. The error appears in a downstream module that didn't change
3. The error message says "class loading failed" not "missing CDI producer"

The natural debugging path ("what changed in the failing module?") leads nowhere
because nothing changed there. The real cause is a new injection point in an
upstream library that Jandex made visible to the downstream module's augmentation.

### Alternatives considered

- **`quarkus-rest-jackson`** — provides the producer but also pulls in REST
  infrastructure (`quarkus-rest`), which is unwanted in a library module
- **`@DefaultBean` ObjectMapper producer in the library** — would work but
  creates a separate ObjectMapper instance, defeating the purpose of injecting
  the app's shared mapper (GE-20260621-629712 rule 1)
- **Making ObjectMapper optional via `Instance<ObjectMapper>`** — adds
  complexity; the adapter always needs an ObjectMapper, so optional lookup
  is misleading

**See also:** [GE-20260505-48085a](GE-20260505-48085a.md) — static ObjectMapper silently fails Instant serialization (related: why injection matters) | [GE-20260621-629712](GE-20260621-629712.md) — canonical CloudEvent adapter pattern rule 1: ObjectMapper must be injected
